segments.label: §56, de source block1
segments.text: Der Einfluss des Lautsystems erstreckt sich über die ganze Sprache, und ein sorgfältiges Studium aller Eigenthümlichkeiten desselben ist die Grundlage jeder genauen Sprachuntersuchung.

segments.label: §56, de source block2
segments.text: Ohne die vollständige Kenntniss der Lautbehandlung, der Verhältnisse und Verwandtschaft der Buchstaben, die in jeder Sprache andren Gesetzen und Gewohnheiten unterliegen, bleibt die Erklärung der grammatischen Formen und das Eingehen in das Ganze des Sprachsystems allemal mangelhaft. (29.)

segments.label: §56, de source block3
segments.text: Unmittelbar beruht auf dem Lautsystem die Verständlichkeit, der Nachdruck und der Wohllaut der Rede, es wirkt aber zugleich auf die reine und feine Intellectualitaet der Sprache, und hierin ist seine Wichtigkeit bisher vielleicht nicht hinlänglich gewürdigt worden.

segments.label: §56, de source block4
segments.text: Sie leuchtet aber sogleich ein, als man sich daran erinnert, dass (21.) der ganze Begriff der Sprache in dem des articulirten Lautes liegt, und dass die Art, wie jede Sprache diesen Begriff auffasst, sich in ihrem Alphabet, als dem System ihrer articulirten Laute darstellt.

segments.label: §56, codex source block1
segments.text: The influence of the sound system extends throughout language, and a careful study of all its peculiarities is the foundation of every exact investigation of language.

segments.label: §56, codex source block2
segments.text: Without a complete knowledge of the treatment of sounds and of the relations and affinities of letters, which are subject to different laws and habits in every language, the explanation of grammatical forms and the exploration of the linguistic system as a whole always remain deficient. (29.)

segments.label: §56, codex source block3
segments.text: The intelligibility, force and euphony of discourse depend directly on the sound system, but it also affects the pure and refined intellectuality of language, and in this respect its importance has perhaps not yet been adequately appreciated.

segments.label: §56, codex source block4
segments.text: Yet this importance becomes immediately apparent when we recall that (21.) the whole concept of language lies in that of articulated sound, and that each language’s way of apprehending this concept is manifested in its alphabet, as the system of its articulated sounds.

segments.label: §56, muse source block1
segments.text: The influence of the sound system extends over the whole of language, and a careful study of all its peculiarities is the foundation of every exact investigation of language.

segments.label: §56, muse source block2
segments.text: Without complete knowledge of the treatment of sounds, of the relations and kinship of the letters, which in every language are subject to other laws and habits, the explanation of grammatical forms and entry into the whole of the language system remain at all times defective. (29.)

segments.label: §56, muse source block3
segments.text: Intelligibility, emphasis, and euphony of speech rest immediately on the sound system, but it also acts at the same time on the pure and refined intellectuality of language, and in this respect its importance has hitherto perhaps not been sufficiently appreciated.

segments.label: §56, muse source block4
segments.text: It becomes evident at once, however, as soon as one recalls that (21.) the whole concept of language lies in that of articulated sound, and that the way in which each language apprehends this concept presents itself in its alphabet, as the system of its articulated sounds.

segments.label: §57, de source block1
segments.text: Das erste ist die Absonderung des Tones von allem mitschallendem Geräusch, welche ihn auf einen wahren Sprachlaut zurückführt.

segments.label: §57, de source block2
segments.text: Er soll nur den Begriff anregen, aus dem er entspringt, und darf nicht mehr Körper besitzen, als dazu erforderlich ist.

segments.label: §57, de source block3
segments.text: Gerade mit dem wenigsten tritt das Charakteristische am schärfsten hervor.

segments.label: §57, de source block4
segments.text: Indem der Geist den thierischen Laut durchdringt, wird dieser zum articulirten, verliert aber nicht in allen Sprachen (28.) seine ursprüngliche Natur ganz und rein, sondern mischt den Tönen ein Schnalzen, Schmettern, Zischen, Schnarren oder Hauchen bei, was man in einigen, vorzüglich Afrikanischen Sprachen in grosser Rohheit, aber in feineren Spuren auch in hoch ausgebildeten antrifft.

segments.label: §57, de source block5
segments.text: Stumpfheit des geistigen Sprachdranges und physische Rauhigkeit der Organe mögen in solchen Fällen zusammenwirken, aber Geist und Organe verfeinern sich durch gegenseitige Einwirkung auf einander, und die Rauhigkeit der Töne schleift sich daher oft in der Fortbildung der Sprachen durch die Zeit allmählich ab.

segments.label: §57, codex source block1
segments.text: The first step is to separate the tone from all accompanying noise, thereby reducing it to a true speech sound.

segments.label: §57, codex source block2
segments.text: It should evoke only the concept from which it springs, and must possess no more body than is required for this.

segments.label: §57, codex source block3
segments.text: It is precisely with the least body that its distinctive character emerges most sharply.

segments.label: §57, codex source block4
segments.text: As the mind penetrates the animal sound, the latter becomes articulated; but not in every language (28.) does it wholly and purely lose its original nature: instead, it mingles the tones with clicking, blaring, hissing, rasping or breathing, which we encounter in great crudity in some languages, especially African ones, but also in finer traces in highly developed languages.

segments.label: §57, codex source block5
segments.text: Dullness of the mind’s impulse towards language and physical roughness of the organs may act together in such cases; but mind and organs refine one another through their mutual influence, and the roughness of the tones is therefore often gradually worn away over time as languages develop.

segments.label: §57, muse source block2
segments.text: It is to arouse only the concept from which it springs, and must possess no more body than is required for that.

segments.label: §57, muse source block3
segments.text: It is precisely with the least that what is characteristic comes out most sharply.

segments.label: §57, muse source block4
segments.text: As the mind permeates the animal sound, the latter becomes articulated sound, but in not all languages (28.) does it lose its original nature wholly and purely; rather, it mixes into the tones a clicking, blaring, hissing, snarling, or breathing, which is met with in great crudity in some, especially African, languages, but in finer traces also in highly developed ones.

segments.label: §57, muse source block5
segments.text: Dulness of the mental impulse towards language and physical roughness of the organs may co-operate in such cases, but mind and organs refine themselves through reciprocal action on each other, and the roughness of the tones therefore often wears away gradually, in the course of time, in the further development of languages.

segments.label: §58, de source block1
segments.text: Allein auch die wirklichen, von mitschallendem Geräusch gereinigten Sprachlaute müssen bestimmt von einander geschieden seyn, nicht einer in den andren hinübertönen.

segments.label: §58, de source block2
segments.text: Die Buchstaben liegen nicht gleichsam bestimmt geschieden in den Sprachwerkzeugen.

segments.label: §58, de source block3
segments.text: Man muss sich vielmehr die Bewegung derselben, welche einer bestimmten Gattung das Daseyn giebt, als ein Continuum denken, wo in jedem Punkte durch plötzliche Fixirung der Laut eine um ein wenig verschiedene Beschaffenheit erhalten würde, je nachdem z. B. die Lippen sich mehr oder weniger öffnen, die Zunge schneller oder langsamer, fester oder leiser, mit schmalerer oder breiterer Fläche anschlägt u. s. f.

segments.label: §58, de source block4
segments.text: Jeder Laut hat mithin eine eigne Sphäre, in welcher er einen bestimmten, aber bei weitem nicht den einzig möglichen Punkt einnimmt.

segments.label: §58, de source block5
segments.text: Diesen Punkt weist ihm die sich bildende Gewohnheit der Nation an, so entsteht ihr besondres Alphabet, und über dieser Entstehung kann Glück und Misgeschick walten.

segments.label: §58, codex source block1
segments.text: But even genuine speech sounds, purified of accompanying noise, must be distinctly separated from one another, rather than letting one shade audibly into another.

segments.label: §58, codex source block2
segments.text: Letters do not lie, as it were, distinctly separated in the organs of speech.

segments.label: §58, codex source block3
segments.text: Rather, we must conceive the movement of these organs that brings a particular kind of sound into being as a continuum, at any point in which a sudden fixing would give the sound a slightly different character, according, for example, to whether the lips open more or less, the tongue strikes more quickly or slowly, more firmly or gently, with a narrower or broader surface, and so forth.

segments.label: §58, codex source block4
segments.text: Every sound thus has a sphere of its own, within which it occupies a definite point, though by no means the only possible one.

segments.label: §58, codex source block5
segments.text: The developing habit of the nation assigns it this point; this is how the nation’s particular alphabet arises, and good or ill fortune may preside over its emergence.

segments.label: §58, muse source block1
segments.text: But even the real speech sounds, purified of accompanying noise, must be definitely separated from one another; one must not sound over into another.

segments.label: §58, muse source block2
segments.text: The letters do not lie, as it were, definitely separated in the organs of speech.

segments.label: §58, muse source block3
segments.text: Rather, one must think of their movement, which gives existence to a definite kind, as a continuum in which at every point, by sudden fixation, the sound would receive a character differing by a little, according as, for example, the lips open more or less, the tongue strikes more quickly or more slowly, more firmly or more softly, with a narrower or broader surface, and so on.

segments.label: §58, muse source block4
segments.text: Every sound thus has its own sphere, in which it occupies a definite point, but by far not the only possible one.

segments.label: §58, muse source block5
segments.text: The nation's habit, as it forms itself, assigns this point to it; in this way its particular alphabet arises, and fortune and misfortune can hold sway over this arising.

segments.label: §58, astra source block1
segments.text: But even actual speech sounds, purified of accompanying noise, must be distinctly separated from one another, without one running into another.

segments.label: §58, astra source block2
segments.text: The letters do not lie, as it were, distinctly separated in the speech organs.

segments.label: §58, astra source block5

segments.label: §59, de source block1
segments.text: Der Einfluss mangelnder reiner Geschiedenheit der Töne wirkt aber noch weit über die blosse Gefahr des Misverständnisses hinaus.

segments.label: §59, de source block2
segments.text: Der articulirte Laut ist zu enge mit dem Geiste verschwistert, als dass nicht seine richtige und fehlerhafte Bildung immer wieder einen entsprechenden Einfluss auf denselben ausüben, dass dieser sich nicht wieder auch in der Rückwirkung des Geistes zeigen, und auf diese Weise nicht eine bis ins Unendliche fortgehende Wechselwirkung entstehen sollte, in welche der Geist zwar seine reinere Natur immer siegend hineinträgt, aber in diesem Uebergewicht immer wieder in etwas durch den widerstrebenden Stoff gehemmt wird.

segments.label: §59, de source block3
segments.text: Reine Bestimmtheit, glückliche Klarheit, eindringende Schärfe der Begriffe in einer Nation hängen daher gar sehr von der reinen Geschiedenheit der Grundlaute ihres Alphabetes ab.

segments.label: §59, codex source block1
segments.text: The influence of a lack of clear separation between tones, however, extends far beyond the mere danger of misunderstanding.

segments.label: §59, codex source block2
segments.text: Articulated sound is too closely akin to the mind for its correct or faulty formation not to exert a corresponding influence on the mind in turn, for this influence not to manifest itself again in the mind’s reaction, and for an interaction continuing to infinity not to arise in this way: into this interaction the mind always brings its purer nature victoriously, yet even in its ascendancy it is repeatedly checked to some degree by the resistant material.

segments.label: §59, codex source block3
segments.text: The pure definiteness, felicitous clarity and penetrating sharpness of a nation’s concepts therefore depend very greatly on the clear separation of the fundamental sounds of its alphabet.

segments.label: §59, muse source block1
segments.text: But the influence of a lack of pure separateness of the tones acts far beyond the mere danger of misunderstanding.

segments.label: §59, muse source block2
segments.text: Articulated sound is too intimately akin, as a sister, to the mind for its correct and faulty formation not always in turn to exert a corresponding influence on the mind, for this influence not in turn also to show itself in the mind's reaction, and for there not in this way to arise a reciprocal action proceeding to infinity, into which the mind indeed always carries its purer nature victoriously, but in this preponderance is always again to some extent impeded by the resistant material.

segments.label: §59, muse source block3
segments.text: Pure definiteness, happy clarity, and penetrating sharpness of concepts in a nation therefore depend very much on the pure separateness of the fundamental sounds of its alphabet.

segments.label: §59, astra source block1
segments.text: The influence of a lack of clean separation between sounds, however, extends far beyond the mere danger of misunderstanding.

segments.label: §59, astra source block2
segments.text: Articulated sound is too closely akin to the mind for its correct or faulty formation not to exert a corresponding influence on it time and again. This influence must in turn show itself in the mind’s reaction, giving rise to an interaction that continues to infinity: the mind always brings its purer nature into it victoriously, yet its ascendancy is repeatedly checked to some extent by the resisting matter.

segments.label: §60, de source block1
segments.text: Es giebt, auch im Gebrauche der blossen articulirten Laute, ohne alle musikalische oder dichterische Beziehung, ein aesthetisches Gefühl, durch das eine Nation getrieben wird, jeden, ihm sein volles Recht einräumend, ganz und hell austönen zu lassen, indem eine andre, welcher dies Gefühl mangelt, oder die dasselbe andren Rücksichten, wie im Englischen der Gewalt des Accents, unterordnet, viele verschluckt, verschmilzt oder verdunkelt.

segments.label: §60, de source block2
segments.text: Hiervon lässt sich in Rücksicht auf die Begriffe dasselbe, als von dem Mangel an richtiger Geschiedenheit sagen.

segments.label: §60, de source block3
segments.text: Es kommt alsdann darauf an, wie dasjenige, was den Begriffen dadurch an ruhig leuchtender Klarheit entgeht, auf andre Weise ersetzt wird.

segments.label: §60, codex source block1
segments.text: Even in the use of articulated sounds alone, without any musical or poetic reference, there is an aesthetic feeling that impels one nation to allow each sound its full due and let it ring out fully and brightly, whereas another nation, which lacks this feeling or subordinates it to other considerations, as in English to the power of accent, swallows, merges or obscures many sounds.

segments.label: §60, codex source block2
segments.text: With regard to concepts, the same may be said of this as of the lack of proper separation.

segments.label: §60, codex source block3
segments.text: The question then is how the calmly shining clarity thereby lost to concepts is made good in other ways.

segments.label: §60, muse source block1
segments.text: Even in the use of mere articulated sounds, without any musical or poetic relation, there is an aesthetic feeling by which one nation is driven, granting each sound its full right, to let it sound out fully and brightly, whereas another, which lacks this feeling or subordinates it to other considerations, as in English to the force of the accent, swallows, fuses, or obscures many of them.

segments.label: §60, muse source block2
segments.text: Of this, with regard to concepts, the same may be said as of the lack of correct separateness.

segments.label: §60, muse source block3
segments.text: It then depends on how what concepts thereby lose in calmly luminous clarity is replaced in another way.

segments.label: §60, astra source block1
segments.text: Even in the use of articulated sounds alone, without any musical or poetic connection, there is an aesthetic feeling that impels one nation to let each sound ring out fully and brightly, giving it its full due, while another nation, lacking this feeling or subordinating it to other considerations, such as the force of accent in English, swallows, fuses or obscures many sounds.

segments.label: §60, astra source block2
segments.text: With regard to concepts, the same can be said of this as of the lack of proper separation.

segments.label: §60, astra source block3
segments.text: What then matters is how the quietly shining clarity that concepts lose in this way is made up for by other means.

segments.label: §61, de source block1
segments.text: Durch den Gebrauch der Sprache entsteht, und zwar in dem Grade mehr, in welchem irgend eine ein glücklich gewähltes Lautsystem richtig anwendet, im Geiste Sinn für feine Lautunterscheidung und Wohlgefallen daran.

segments.label: §61, de source block2
segments.text: Da nun die Rede auch vieler Unterscheidungen bedarf, um die Begriffe in allen ihren Verhältnissen und Schattirungen auszudrücken und anzuregen, so kommt jener Sinn diesem Bedürfniss sehr glücklich zu Statten.

segments.label: §61, de source block3
segments.text: Denn es geht nun Neigung und Fähigkeit hervor, diese Unterschiede durch einzelne Buchstabenveränderung zu bezeichnen, und an ihr zu erkennen, worin der Ursprung aller Inflexion liegt, man mag sie nun für gleichzeitig mit der Sprache, oder für später in ihr entstanden halten.

segments.label: §61, de source block4
segments.text: Es wird aber durch sie der doppelte Vorzug gewonnen, der Idee nur gerade soviel Körper zu geben, als sie bedarf, und durch den in sich selbst ganz bedeutungslosen Buchstaben, jeden irre leitenden Nebenbegriff zu vermeiden.

segments.label: §61, de source block5
segments.text: Es liegt in der Sprache ein durch alle ihre Functionen gehendes und sich immer steigerndes Streben nach Läuterung der Intellectualität.

segments.label: §61, de source block6
segments.text: So wie sie (57.) von dem Sprachlaut das mitschallende Geräusch absondert, so entfernt sie auch in dem durch Sprache Gedachten die Vorstellung jedes nicht durch den Gedanken nothwendig werdenden Stoffs, und verdrängt ihn da, wo er als Zeichen der Form auftreten will, durch den bedeutungslosen Laut.

segments.label: §61, de source block7
segments.text: Es ist daher eine Eigenschaft aller für den Geist angemessner gebildeten Sprachen, wenn man sie mit andren, ihnen darin entgegengesetzten vergleicht, eine geringere Masse des Stoffes bei dem Ausdruck derselben Idee anzuregen, und diese dadurch freier und geläuterter hervortreten zu lassen.

segments.label: §61, codex source block1
segments.text: The use of language produces in the mind a sense for fine distinctions of sound and a pleasure in them, and does so to a greater degree the more correctly a language employs a well-chosen sound system.

segments.label: §61, codex source block2
segments.text: Since discourse also needs many distinctions in order to express and evoke concepts in all their relations and shades, this sense serves that need most happily.

segments.label: §61, codex source block3
segments.text: For there now arise an inclination and an ability to mark these differences through changes of individual letters and to recognise them by those changes; in this lies the origin of all inflection, whether we regard it as arising simultaneously with language or later within it.

segments.label: §61, codex source block4
segments.text: Through inflection, however, a double advantage is gained: the idea is given only just as much body as it requires, and the letter, which is entirely meaningless in itself, avoids every misleading subsidiary concept.

segments.label: §61, codex source block5
segments.text: There is in language a striving towards the purification of intellectuality that runs through all its functions and continually intensifies.

segments.label: §61, codex source block6
segments.text: Just as language (57.) separates accompanying noise from the speech sound, so too, in what is thought through language, it removes the representation of any material not made necessary by the thought, and wherever such material seeks to appear as a sign of form, it displaces it with meaningless sound.

segments.label: §61, codex source block7
segments.text: It is therefore a property of all languages more suitably formed for the mind, when compared with others opposed to them in this respect, to evoke a smaller mass of material in expressing the same idea, and thereby to let the idea emerge more freely and in greater purity.

segments.label: §61, muse source block1
segments.text: Through the use of language there arises in the mind, and indeed to a greater degree in proportion as any language rightly applies a happily chosen sound system, a sense for fine discrimination of sounds and pleasure in it.

segments.label: §61, muse source block2
segments.text: Now, since speech also needs many distinctions in order to express and arouse concepts in all their relations and shadings, that sense comes very happily to the aid of this need.

segments.label: §61, muse source block3
segments.text: For there now proceeds from it an inclination and ability to designate these differences by change of a single letter and to recognize them by it, in which lies the origin of all inflexion, whether one regards it as simultaneous with language or as having arisen later in it.

segments.label: §61, muse source block4
segments.text: But through it the double advantage is gained of giving the idea only just as much body as it needs, and, through the letter, in itself quite meaningless, of avoiding every misleading subsidiary concept.

segments.label: §61, muse source block5
segments.text: There lies in language a striving after purification of intellectuality, proceeding through all its functions and ever increasing.

segments.label: §61, muse source block6
segments.text: Just as it (57.) separates the accompanying noise from the speech sound, so also in what is thought through language it removes the representation of every material not made necessary by the thought, and displaces it, where it wants to appear as a sign of form, by the meaningless sound.

segments.label: §61, muse source block7
segments.text: It is therefore a property of all languages formed more appropriately for the mind, when one compares them with others opposite to them in this respect, to arouse a smaller mass of material in the expression of the same idea, and thereby to let the latter emerge more freely and in a more purified form.

segments.label: §62, de source block1
segments.text: Es ist eine natürliche und fast nothwendige Folge der reinen Scheidung der Töne, dass das Alphabet dadurch mehr Umfang erhält.

segments.label: §62, de source block2
segments.text: Denn die Töne, welche das Ohr bei dunkler, unausgebildeter Aussprache leicht verwechseln konnte, treten nun bestimmt aus einander.

segments.label: §62, de source block3
segments.text: Bisweilen entsteht aber auch die Verschiedenheit des Umfanges des Alphabets aus besondren Lauteigenthümlichkeiten und Gewohnheiten der Nationen, durch welche demselben einzelne Buchstaben, wie das gestrichene Polnische l, und sogar ganze Classen derselben, wie die Indischen Cerebralen oder Lingualen zuwachsen.

segments.label: §62, de source block4
segments.text: Die Lage und Bewegung der Sprachwerkzeuge, und das Fallen der einzelnen Töne in dieselben oder verschiedene Sphären (58.) macht, dass die Buchstaben in gegenseitigen Beziehungen und Verhältnissen zu einander stehn, und in dem Alphabet ein mehr oder minder vollständiges System von Tönen entdeckt werden kann.

segments.label: §62, de source block5
segments.text: Nach einmal entstandener Schrift und bei hinzutretender grammatischer Behandlung kann ein Alphabet in dieser Beziehung ein fester bestimmtes und feiner ausgebildetes System erhalten, als ursprünglich in dem Sprachgebrauch der Nation lag, und so mag es dem Sanskrita Alphabet, dessen Typus sich über die noch lebenden Sprachen eines grossen Theils von Süd-Asien verbreitet hat, ergangen seyn.

segments.label: §62, de source block6
segments.text: Allein der Totalitaet nach liegt ein solches System immer in den Sprachanlagen und Sprachgewohnheiten der Nationen, und die Bestimmtheit, welche es allerdings durch glücklich gewählte Schriftzeichen gewinnt, wirkt wieder auf das Sprechen zurück, und verwandelt sich in ihr wahres Eigenthum.

segments.label: §62, codex source block1
segments.text: It is a natural and almost necessary consequence of the clear separation of tones that the alphabet thereby gains in range.

segments.label: §62, codex source block2
segments.text: For tones that the ear could easily confuse in obscure, undeveloped pronunciation now stand distinctly apart.

segments.label: §62, codex source block3
segments.text: Sometimes, however, differences in the range of the alphabet also arise from nations’ particular peculiarities and habits of sound, through which individual letters, such as the Polish l with a stroke, and even whole classes of letters, such as the Indian cerebrals or linguals, are added to it.

segments.label: §62, codex source block4
segments.text: The position and movement of the organs of speech, and the fact that individual tones fall within the same or different spheres (58.), mean that letters stand in mutual relations and proportions, and that a more or less complete system of tones can be discovered in the alphabet.

segments.label: §62, codex source block5
segments.text: Once writing has arisen and grammatical treatment is added, an alphabet can acquire in this respect a more firmly determined and more finely developed system than originally existed in the nation’s linguistic usage; this may have happened to the Sanskrit alphabet, whose pattern has spread across the still living languages of a large part of southern Asia.

segments.label: §62, codex source block6
segments.text: Yet in its totality such a system always lies in nations’ linguistic dispositions and habits, and the definiteness it admittedly gains through well-chosen written signs acts back upon speaking and becomes the nations’ true possession.

segments.label: §62, muse source block1
segments.text: It is a natural and almost necessary consequence of the pure separation of the tones that the alphabet thereby receives greater extent.

segments.label: §62, muse source block2
segments.text: For the tones which the ear could easily confuse in obscure, undeveloped pronunciation now step definitely apart from one another.

segments.label: §62, muse source block3
segments.text: Sometimes, however, the difference in the extent of the alphabet also arises from particular sound peculiarities and habits of nations, by which single letters, such as the barred Polish l, and even whole classes of them, such as the Indian cerebrals or linguals, accrue to it.

segments.label: §62, muse source block4
segments.text: The position and movement of the organs of speech, and the falling of the individual tones into the same or different spheres (58.), cause the letters to stand in reciprocal connections and relations to one another, and allow a more or less complete system of tones to be discovered in the alphabet.

segments.label: §62, muse source block5
segments.text: After writing has once arisen, and with grammatical treatment added, an alphabet can in this respect receive a more firmly definite and more finely developed system than originally lay in the nation's linguistic usage, and this may have been the case with the Sanskrit alphabet, whose type has spread over the still living languages of a great part of southern Asia.

segments.label: §62, muse source block6
segments.text: But as a totality such a system always lies in the nations' dispositions and habits for language, and the definiteness which it admittedly gains through happily chosen written characters reacts in turn upon speaking and is transformed into their true property.

segments.label: §62, astra source block1
segments.text: A natural and almost necessary consequence of the clean separation of sounds is that it increases the range of the alphabet.

segments.label: §62, astra source block2
segments.text: For sounds that the ear could easily confuse in indistinct, undeveloped pronunciation now stand distinctly apart.

segments.label: §62, astra source block3
segments.text: Sometimes, however, differences in the range of the alphabet also arise from particular sound peculiarities and habits of nations, through which individual letters, such as the Polish l with a stroke, and even whole classes of letters, such as the Indian cerebrals or linguals, are added to it.

segments.label: §62, astra source block4
segments.text: The position and movement of the speech organs, and the fact that individual sounds fall within the same or different spheres (58.), mean that the letters have mutual connections and relations, and that a more or less complete system of sounds can be discovered in the alphabet.

segments.label: §62, astra source block5
segments.text: Once writing has come into being, and grammatical study has been added to it, an alphabet can acquire in this respect a more firmly defined and finely developed system than was originally present in the nation’s language use. This may have happened to the Sanskrit alphabet, whose pattern has spread to the languages still living in a large part of South Asia.

segments.label: §62, astra source block6
segments.text: Yet in its totality such a system always lies within nations’ capacities for language and habits of language use; and the definiteness that it admittedly gains through well-chosen written signs acts back upon speaking and becomes truly the nations’ own.

segments.label: §62a, de source block1
segments.text: Bei der Verbindung mehrerer Buchstaben zur Sylbe zeigen sich neue Eigenthümlichkeiten des Lautsystems, je nachdem die Sprachen das Zusammentreffen einiger Buchstaben begünstigen, andrer vermeiden, und eine Anzahl von Sylben ausstossen.

segments.label: §62a, de source block2
segments.text: Man hat daher, ausser dem Umfange des Alphabets, auch auf den der durch dasselbe möglichen Sylben zu achten.

segments.label: §62a, de source block3
segments.text: Es ist bemerkenswerth, dass gerade die Sprachen der Wilden, die man wohl der Rauhigkeit zu beschuldigen pflegt, viele Sylben ausstossen, die in hochgebildeten Sprachen geduldet werden.

segments.label: §62a, de source block4
segments.text: Es mag dies zum Theil aus der schon im Vorigen bemerkten reizbareren Empfindlichkeit der Sinne dieser Völker, und zum Theil daraus herrühren, dass die gebildetere Sprache oft Sylben zusammenzieht, wo die ursprünglichere jede für sich auf einander folgen lässt.

segments.label: §62a, codex source block1
segments.text: When several letters are combined into a syllable, new peculiarities of the sound system become apparent, according to whether languages favour the coming together of certain letters, avoid that of others, and exclude a number of syllables.

segments.label: §62a, codex source block2
segments.text: Besides the range of the alphabet, we must therefore also attend to the range of syllables possible through it.

segments.label: §62a, codex source block3
segments.text: It is remarkable that precisely the languages of savages, which people are apt to accuse of roughness, exclude many syllables tolerated in highly cultivated languages.

segments.label: §62a, codex source block4
segments.text: This may arise partly from the more readily excited sensitivity of these peoples’ senses, already noted above, and partly from the fact that the more cultivated language often contracts syllables where the more original language lets each follow separately in succession.

segments.label: §62a, muse source block1
segments.text: In the combination of several letters into a syllable, new peculiarities of the sound system show themselves, according as languages favour the meeting of some letters, avoid that of others, and reject a number of syllables.

segments.label: §62a, muse source block2
segments.text: Apart from the extent of the alphabet, one must therefore also attend to that of the syllables possible through it.

segments.label: §62a, muse source block3
segments.text: It is remarkable that precisely the languages of savages, which one is wont to accuse of roughness, reject many syllables that are tolerated in highly cultivated languages.

segments.label: §62a, muse source block4
segments.text: This may stem partly from the more irritable sensibility of the senses of these peoples, already remarked on earlier, and partly from the fact that the more cultivated language often contracts syllables where the more original one lets each follow another separately.

segments.label: §62b, de source block1
segments.text: Auch die Wortbildung unterliegt Regeln des Lautsystems, da in vielen Sprachen die Wörter mit gewissen Buchstaben nicht anfangen oder enden, und auch ihr innerer Bau durch Sprachgesetze, namentlich in der Verwandlung zusammenstossender Consonanten, bestimmt wird.

segments.label: §62b, codex source block1
segments.text: Word formation, too, is subject to rules of the sound system, since in many languages words do not begin or end with certain letters, and their internal structure is also determined by linguistic laws, notably in the transformation of consonants that come together.

segments.label: §62b, muse source block1
segments.text: Word-formation also is subject to rules of the sound system, since in many languages words do not begin or end with certain letters, and their internal structure too is determined by laws of language, namely in the transformation of consonants that come together.

segments.label: §63, de source block1
segments.text: In diesen Systemen liegen die Gründe und die Bedingungen der Buchstabenveränderung, die gleichfalls nur zum Theil durch die allgemeinere Natur der Sprachwerkzeuge gegeben ist, ausserdem aber auf den besondren Lautgewohnheiten jedes Volkes beruht.

segments.label: §63, de source block2
segments.text: Denn wenn die Natur der Buchstaben auch die Art der Verwandlung bestimmt, so hängt es von dem Ohr und den Sprachwerkzeugen jedes Volkes ab, wie empfindlich es für diesen gegenseitigen Einfluss der Laute auf einander bei ihrer Berührung ist.

segments.label: §63, de source block3
segments.text: Je näher sich in einem sehr systematischen Alphabet von bedeutendem Umfange die Töne stehen, und je klarer und bestimmter in einem solchen ihr Verhältniss erkannt wird, desto mehr wächst die Neigung zur Buchstabenverwandlung, so wie hinwiederum sie gar sehr zur feineren Lautunterscheidung und zur Systematisirung des Alphabets beiträgt.

segments.label: §63, de source block4
segments.text: Man könnte glauben, dass das Ohr uncultivirter Nationen diese Feinheiten der Töne überhörte und vernachlässigte, man findet aber gerade bei ihnen sehr häufige Buchstabenverwandlungen, was den beiden Ursachen zuzuschreiben seyn mag, dass gerade die Sinne des der Natur näher stehenden Menschen eine schärfere Empfindlichkeit besitzen, und dass der Uncultivirte die Rede vor dem Verstände wie ein sich überall berührendes Continuum ansieht, indess der Gebildete auch in der fortlaufenden Rede das Verschleifen der Töne nach den Pausen des Verstandes durch die Zunge hemmt.

segments.label: §63, de source block5
segments.text: Aber eine wahre Nationaleigenheit der Indischen Völker, für die sich kein weiterer Grund anführen lässt, ist wohl die so häufige Verkettung mehrerer Worte durch Buchstabenverwandlung und Zusammenziehung, von der es wenigstens nicht sichtbar ist, ob auch andre Nationen sie in dem Masse gekannt haben.

segments.label: §63, de source block6
segments.text: Auf den ersten Anblick geräth man in Versuchung die mannigfaltigen im Sanskrit hieraus entstehenden Regeln wenigstens zum Theil der Systemsucht der Grammatiker zuzuschreiben.

segments.label: §63, de source block7
segments.text: Allein diese Vermuthung verschwindet bei der Vergleichung der lebenden, aus dem Sanskrit hervorgegangenen Indischen Sprachen.

segments.label: §63, de source block8
segments.text: Von der Telinga, in welcher diese Verkettung gerade vorzüglich häufig und schwierig zu erkennen ist, sagt Carey ausdrücklich, dass der Fremde, welcher dieselbe vernachlässigen wollte, gar nicht würde von den Eingebornen verstanden werden.

segments.label: §63, de source block9
segments.text: Im Bengalischen dagegen wird sie nicht immer streng beobachtet, so dass man daraus noch deutlicher sieht, wie dieser Punkt von den individuellen Gewohnheiten der Stämme abhängt.

segments.label: §63, codex source block1
segments.text: In these systems lie the grounds and conditions of letter change, which likewise is determined only in part by the more general nature of the organs of speech, but otherwise rests on each people’s particular habits of sound.

segments.label: §63, codex source block2
segments.text: For although the nature of the letters determines the kind of transformation, how sensitive a people is to this mutual influence of sounds upon one another when they come into contact depends on its ear and organs of speech.

segments.label: §63, codex source block3
segments.text: The closer the tones stand to one another in a highly systematic alphabet of considerable range, and the more clearly and distinctly their relationship is recognised in such an alphabet, the more the inclination towards letter transformation grows; conversely, this transformation contributes very greatly to finer distinctions of sound and to the systematisation of the alphabet.

segments.label: §63, codex source block4
segments.text: One might think that the ear of uncultivated nations would fail to hear and would neglect these subtleties of tone; yet it is precisely among them that very frequent letter transformations are found, which may be attributed to two causes: the senses of human beings closer to nature possess a keener sensitivity, and the uncultivated person regards discourse, before the understanding intervenes, as a continuum whose parts are everywhere in contact, whereas the cultivated person uses the tongue, even in continuous discourse, to check the running together of tones in accordance with the pauses of the understanding.

segments.label: §63, codex source block5
segments.text: But the very frequent chaining together of several words through letter transformation and contraction is probably a true national peculiarity of the Indian peoples, for which no further ground can be given; at least, it is not evident whether other nations too have known it to the same extent.

segments.label: §63, codex source block6
segments.text: At first sight one is tempted to attribute the manifold rules arising from this in Sanskrit, at least in part, to the grammarians’ passion for systems.

segments.label: §63, codex source block7
segments.text: But this conjecture disappears when one compares the living Indian languages that have emerged from Sanskrit.

segments.label: §63, codex source block8
segments.text: Of Telinga, in which this chaining is particularly frequent and difficult to recognise, Carey expressly says that a foreigner who chose to neglect it would not be understood by the native inhabitants at all.

segments.label: §63, codex source block9
segments.text: In Bengali, by contrast, it is not always strictly observed, making it still clearer how this point depends on the individual habits of the tribes.

segments.label: §64, de source block1
segments.text: Den nächsten Einfluss hat diese Eigenthümlichkeit natürlich auf den Wohllaut.

segments.label: §64, de source block2
segments.text: Es schmeichelt dem Ohre, wenn das harte Zusammentreffen widerstrebender und unharmonischer Laute möglichst vermieden wird.

segments.label: §64, de source block3
segments.text: Aber die Wirkung erstreckt sich auch auf die ideale Geltung der Sprache, und die richtige Gliederung der Rede vor dem Verstände, dies jedoch nur dann, wenn die Buchstabenveränderung sich begnügt, Theile desselben Worts zu einem Ganzen zu verschmelzen, und nicht durch das Aneinanderreihen ganzer von einander unabhängiger Worte ein Ganzes vor dem Ohre bildet, das vor dem Verstände nicht, als solches, bestehen kann.

segments.label: §64, de source block4
segments.text: Die letztere Gewohnheit kann ich nur insofern für nützlich halten, als sie in der Poesie ein Mittel mehr gewährt, die Worteinschnitte mit den rhythmischen in ein angemessenes Verhältniss zu bringen.

segments.label: §64, de source block5
segments.text: Es entstehen nemlich dadurch andre, und häufiger grössere Lautganze, als die blosse Worteintheilung gewährt.

segments.label: §64, de source block6
segments.text: Dagegen ist es für den Verstand und das Ohr störend, wenn sich der Endbuchstabe durch Veränderung da auf den ihm nachfolgenden vorbereitet, wo der Verstand logisch und das Ohr rhythmisch eine Pause verlangt.

segments.label: §64, de source block7
segments.text: Beschränkt sich hingegen diese Lautverwandlung auf die Gränzen des Wortes, so wird sie zu einem phonetischen Mittel, die Rede in rein geschiedene Ganze zu zertheilen, und prägt dem Verstände auch sinnlich ein, dass das Element der Rede das Wort ist.

segments.label: §64, de source block8
segments.text: Die logische Gliederung derselben erfährt keine Störung, sondern wird gelegentlich, so oft nemlich eine solche Lautveränderung eintritt, noch herausgehoben.

segments.label: §64, de source block9
segments.text: Diesen Grundsatz der Nothwendigkeit, die Wortganze durch besondre Toneinheit zu charakterisiren, verkennt zwar auch die Sanskrita Sprache nicht, da in ihr andre Regeln für die Mitte der Wörter, als für das Zusammenstossen zweier gelten.

segments.label: §64, de source block10
segments.text: Da aber diese Regeln in Einigem übereinkommen, und die für mehrere Worte auch für die Theile zusammengesetzter Wörter gelten, so erscheint die Wortabtheilung durch dies Mittel nicht in rein geschiedener sinnlicher Klarheit.

segments.label: §64, codex source block1
segments.text: The most immediate influence of this peculiarity is naturally on euphony.

segments.label: §64, codex source block2
segments.text: It pleases the ear when the harsh collision of resistant and inharmonious sounds is avoided as far as possible.

segments.label: §64, codex source block3
segments.text: But the effect also extends to language’s efficacy in the realm of ideas and to the proper articulation of discourse for the understanding, though only when letter change confines itself to merging parts of the same word into a whole, rather than joining entire, mutually independent words in a sequence to form a whole for the ear that cannot subsist as such for the understanding.

segments.label: §64, codex source block4
segments.text: I can regard the latter habit as useful only in so far as, in poetry, it provides one more means of bringing word divisions into an appropriate relationship with rhythmic divisions.

segments.label: §64, codex source block5
segments.text: For it produces different, and more often larger, wholes of sound than division into words alone provides.

segments.label: §64, codex source block6
segments.text: By contrast, it disturbs both the understanding and the ear when a final letter prepares itself through change for the letter following it at a point where the understanding logically, and the ear rhythmically, demands a pause.

segments.label: §64, codex source block7
segments.text: If, however, this sound transformation confines itself within the boundaries of the word, it becomes a phonetic means of dividing discourse into clearly separated wholes, and impresses upon the understanding, through the senses too, that the element of discourse is the word.

segments.label: §64, codex source block8
segments.text: The logical articulation of discourse suffers no disturbance, but is occasionally given further prominence, namely whenever such a sound change occurs.

segments.label: §64, codex source block9
segments.text: Sanskrit, too, acknowledges this principle that word wholes must be characterised by a distinct unity of tone, since it has different rules for the interior of words and for the meeting of two words.

segments.label: §64, codex source block10
segments.text: But since these rules agree in some respects, and those for several words also apply to the parts of compound words, this means does not make word division manifest with clearly differentiated sensory clarity.

segments.label: §64, muse source block1
segments.text: Naturally, this peculiarity has its nearest influence on euphony.

segments.label: §64, muse source block2
segments.text: It flatters the ear when the harsh meeting of resistant and unharmonious sounds is avoided as far as possible.

segments.label: §64, muse source block3
segments.text: But the effect also extends to the ideal validity of language and the correct articulation of speech before the understanding, though only when letter-change contents itself with fusing parts of the same word into a whole, and does not, by stringing together whole words independent of one another, form before the ear a whole that cannot, as such, subsist before the understanding.

segments.label: §64, muse source block4
segments.text: The latter habit I can regard as useful only in so far as it affords in poetry one means more of bringing the word-breaks into a fitting relation with the rhythmical breaks.

segments.label: §64, muse source block5
segments.text: For thereby other, and more often larger, wholes of sound arise than mere division into words affords.

segments.label: §64, muse source block6
segments.text: On the other hand, it is disturbing for the understanding and the ear when the final letter, by change, prepares itself for the one following it at a place where the understanding logically and the ear rhythmically demand a pause.

segments.label: §64, muse source block7
segments.text: If, by contrast, this sound-transformation is restricted to the limits of the word, it becomes a phonetic means of dividing speech into purely separated wholes, and impresses also sensibly on the understanding that the element of speech is the word.

segments.label: §64, muse source block8
segments.text: The logical articulation of speech suffers no disturbance, but on occasion, namely as often as such a sound-change occurs, is even thrown into relief.

segments.label: §64, muse source block9
segments.text: The Sanskrit language, it is true, does not fail to recognize this principle of the necessity of characterizing word-wholes by a special unity of tone either, since in it other rules hold for the middle of words than for the coming together of two words.

segments.label: §64, muse source block10
segments.text: But since these rules agree in some respects, and those for several words also hold for the parts of compound words, division into words does not appear by this means in purely separated sensible clarity.

segments.label: §64, astra source block5

segments.label: §64, astra source block6
segments.text: By contrast, it disturbs both the understanding and the ear when a final letter changes in preparation for the one that follows it at a point where the understanding requires a logical pause and the ear a rhythmic one.

segments.label: §64, astra source block7
segments.text: If, however, this sound change remains within the bounds of the word, it becomes a phonetic means of dividing speech into cleanly separated wholes, and impresses upon the understanding, through the senses as well, that the element of speech is the word.

segments.label: §64, astra source block8
segments.text: The logical division of speech suffers no disruption; on occasion, namely whenever such a sound change occurs, it is made still more evident.

segments.label: §64, astra source block9
segments.text: Nor does Sanskrit fail to recognize this principle of the need to characterize words as wholes through a distinct unity of sound, since different rules apply within words from those that apply when two words meet.

segments.label: §64, astra source block10
segments.text: But since these rules agree in some respects, and those for several words also apply to the parts of compound words, word division is not made cleanly distinct and clear to the senses by this means.

segments.label: §65, de source block1
segments.text: Das Zeitmass gehört den Sylben an.

segments.label: §65, de source block2
segments.text: Da aber die Vocale die Sylbe bestimmen, und auch für sich allein bilden können, so wirkt das Gefühl für dieselbe auch auf die Vollständigkeit des Alphabets ein, in dem entweder alle Vocallaute, jeder in seiner Länge oder Kürze, rein geschieden vorkommen, oder nicht.

segments.label: §65, de source block3
segments.text: Doch können die geschriebenen Zeichen nicht allein hierüber entscheiden.

segments.label: §65, de source block4
segments.text: So bleibt es im Sanskrit immer zweifelhaft, ob die lebende Sprache nicht auch ein kurzes e und o besass.

segments.label: §65, de source block5
segments.text: Das Zeitmass liegt ganz und gar in der Natur der Aussprache, und entzieht sich am meisten der willkührlichen Bestimmung.

segments.label: §65, de source block6
segments.text: Selbst individuelle Anlagen und Gewohnheiten können einen geringeren Einfluss darauf ausüben, da z. B. das Zusammenstossen mehrerer Laute nothwendig mehr Zeit in der Aussprache erfordern muss.

segments.label: §65, de source block7
segments.text: Dagegen kann Anlage, Gewohnheit und Absicht in einer Sprache die ganze Geltung des Zeitmasses in der Rede begünstigen, oder beschränken, und hieraus entspringt für den Wohllaut und die rhythmische Schönheit der Rede und der Sprache überhaupt, auch in ihrer Wirkung auf den Charakter, ein höchst wichtiger Unterschied.

segments.label: §65, de source block8
segments.text: Der Ausdruck der Gedanken wird durch diese rhythmische Eigenthümlichkeit der Sprache weniger wesentlich betroffen.

segments.label: §65, de source block9
segments.text: Zu grosse Begünstigung desselben kann ihm niemals nachtheilig werden, ungerechte Vernachlässigung nur insofern, als die nicht sorgfältige Scheidung der langen und kurzen Vocale denselben Nachtheil, als die Verdunkelung des reinen Lauts der Buchstaben überhaupt mit sich führt.

segments.label: §65, de source block10
segments.text: Dagegen kann die Unterdrückung der natürlichen Geltung des Zeitmasses wohl den Gedankenausdruck zu einseitig herausheben.

segments.label: §65, de source block11
segments.text: Denn Rhythmus und Accent stehen in einem Verhältniss zu einander, das da, wo nicht richtige Sprachbehandlung es in schönes Ebenmass ausgleicht, dem ersteren feindselig werden kann, indem es dem ruhigen Walten des Zeitmasses nicht immer gelingt, neben der Heftigkeit der Rede, oder dem scharf accentuirenden Verstände sein Recht zu behaupten.

segments.label: §65, de source block12
segments.text: Das Vorherrschen des aesthetischen Gefühls, das aber ebensowohl in der Einseitigkeit, als der Rohheit Hindernisse finden kann, ist hier entscheidend, erhält seine Freiheit neben dem Nachdruck der Gedankenverbindung, und weist dem Accent selbst im Wort seine dem rhythmischen Wohllaut angemessene Stelle an.

segments.label: §65, codex source block1
segments.text: Temporal measure belongs to syllables.

segments.label: §65, codex source block2
segments.text: But since vowels determine the syllable and can also form one by themselves, the feeling for the syllable also influences the completeness of the alphabet, in which either all vowel sounds occur clearly separated, each in its length or shortness, or they do not.

segments.label: §65, codex source block3
segments.text: Written signs alone, however, cannot decide this.

segments.label: §65, codex source block4
segments.text: Thus in Sanskrit it remains uncertain whether the living language did not also possess a short e and o.

segments.label: §65, codex source block5
segments.text: Temporal measure lies entirely in the nature of pronunciation and is least amenable to arbitrary determination.

segments.label: §65, codex source block6
segments.text: Even individual dispositions and habits can exert comparatively little influence on it, since, for example, the coming together of several sounds must necessarily require more time in pronunciation.

segments.label: §65, codex source block7
segments.text: By contrast, disposition, habit and intention in a language can favour or restrict the overall sway of temporal measure in discourse, and from this arises a difference of the greatest importance for the euphony and rhythmic beauty of discourse and of language generally, including its effect on character.

segments.label: §65, codex source block8
segments.text: The expression of thoughts is less essentially affected by this rhythmic peculiarity of language.

segments.label: §65, codex source block9
segments.text: Excessive favouring of temporal measure can never harm the expression of thoughts; undue neglect can do so only in so far as failure to distinguish long and short vowels carefully entails the same disadvantage as obscuring the pure sound of letters in general.

segments.label: §65, codex source block10
segments.text: By contrast, suppressing the natural sway of temporal measure may well give the expression of thought too one-sided a prominence.

segments.label: §65, codex source block11
segments.text: For rhythm and accent stand in a relationship that can become hostile to the former wherever proper treatment of language does not bring it into beautiful balance, since the calm sway of temporal measure does not always succeed in asserting its rights alongside the vehemence of discourse or the sharply accentuating understanding.

segments.label: §65, codex source block12
segments.text: The predominance of aesthetic feeling, which may, however, encounter obstacles in one-sidedness as well as in crudity, is decisive here: it preserves its freedom alongside the force of the connection of thoughts, and assigns even the accent within the word its place in accordance with rhythmic euphony.

segments.label: §65, muse source block1
segments.text: Time-measure belongs to syllables.

segments.label: §65, muse source block2
segments.text: But since vowels determine the syllable and can also form it by themselves alone, the feeling for it also acts on the completeness of the alphabet, in that either all vowel sounds, each in its length or shortness, occur purely separated, or they do not.

segments.label: §65, muse source block3
segments.text: Yet the written signs cannot alone decide on this.

segments.label: §65, muse source block4
segments.text: Thus in Sanskrit it always remains doubtful whether the living language did not also possess a short e and o.

segments.label: §65, muse source block5
segments.text: Time-measure lies wholly in the nature of pronunciation, and withdraws itself most of all from arbitrary determination.

segments.label: §65, muse source block6
segments.text: Even individual dispositions and habits can exert only a lesser influence on it, since, for example, the coming together of several sounds must necessarily require more time in pronunciation.

segments.label: §65, muse source block7
segments.text: On the other hand, disposition, habit, and intention in a language can favour or restrict the whole validity of time-measure in speech, and from this there arises, for euphony and the rhythmical beauty of speech and of language in general, also in their effect on character, a most important difference.

segments.label: §65, muse source block8
segments.text: The expression of thoughts is less essentially affected by this rhythmical peculiarity of language.

segments.label: §65, muse source block9
segments.text: Too great favouring of it can never become detrimental to it; unjust neglect only in so far as the failure carefully to separate the long and short vowels brings with it the same disadvantage as the obscuring of the pure sound of the letters in general.

segments.label: §65, muse source block10
segments.text: On the other hand, suppression of the natural validity of time-measure may well throw the expression of thought into relief in too one-sided a way.

segments.label: §65, muse source block11
segments.text: For rhythm and accent stand in a relation to one another which, where correct treatment of language does not balance it into beautiful proportion, can become hostile to rhythm, in that the calm prevalence of time-measure does not always succeed in maintaining its right beside the vehemence of speech or the sharply accentuating understanding.

segments.label: §65, muse source block12
segments.text: The predominance of aesthetic feeling, which can however find obstacles in one-sidedness as well as in crudity, is decisive here; it preserves its freedom beside the emphasis of the combination of thoughts, and assigns to accent, even in the word, its place fitting for rhythmical euphony.

segments.label: §65, astra source block1
segments.text: Quantity belongs to syllables.

segments.label: §65, astra source block2
segments.text: But since vowels determine the syllable, and can also form one on their own, the feeling for the syllable also affects the completeness of the alphabet, in which either all vowel sounds occur cleanly distinguished, each in its long or short form, or they do not.

segments.label: §65, astra source block3
segments.text: Written signs alone, however, cannot decide this.

segments.label: §65, astra source block4
segments.text: Thus, in the case of Sanskrit, it remains uncertain whether the living language also possessed a short e and o.

segments.label: §65, astra source block5
segments.text: Quantity lies wholly in the nature of pronunciation and is least amenable to arbitrary determination.

segments.label: §65, astra source block6
segments.text: Even individual dispositions and habits can exert only a lesser influence on it, since, for example, the meeting of several sounds must necessarily require more time in pronunciation.

segments.label: §65, astra source block7
segments.text: By contrast, disposition, habit and intention can favour or restrict the full effect of quantity in a language’s speech; from this arises a difference of the greatest importance for the euphony and rhythmic beauty of speech and of language generally, including their effect on character.

segments.label: §65, astra source block8
segments.text: The expression of thoughts is less fundamentally affected by this rhythmic peculiarity of language.

segments.label: §65, astra source block9
segments.text: Even excessive favour shown to quantity can never harm the expression of thoughts; unwarranted neglect can do so only insofar as a failure to distinguish long and short vowels carefully brings with it the same disadvantage as obscuring the pure sound of letters in general.

segments.label: §65, astra source block10
segments.text: On the other hand, suppressing the natural effect of quantity may well give the expression of thought an excessively one-sided prominence.

segments.label: §65, astra source block11
segments.text: For rhythm and accent stand in a relation that can become hostile to the former wherever proper handling of language fails to bring it into a beautiful balance, since quantity, in its quiet sway, does not always manage to assert its right alongside the vehemence of speech or the sharply accentuating understanding.

segments.label: §65, astra source block12
segments.text: The predominance of aesthetic feeling, which can meet with obstacles in one-sidedness just as much as in crudity, is decisive here: it preserves the freedom of rhythm alongside the emphasis of the connection of thoughts, and assigns accent, even within the word, its place in keeping with rhythmic euphony.

segments.label: §66, de source block1
segments.text: So wie das Zeitmass grösstentheils der eigenthümlichen Natur der Töne, so gehört der Accent ausschliesslich der Absicht des Redenden an.

segments.label: §66, de source block2
segments.text: Er ist das Mittel, durch welches die Sprache die Rede, welche, ohne ihn, aus bloss an einander gereihten Grundtheilen bestehen würde, in verschiedene neben- und untergeordnete Ganze verknüpft und absondert.

segments.label: §66, de source block3
segments.text: Denn indem der Accent eine Sylbe betont, macht er die folgenden tonlos, zieht sie daher in das Gebiet der betonten, und verbindet sie mithin mit derselben.

segments.label: §66, de source block4
segments.text: Ebendies geschieht, wenn man Sylben, welche der Betonung vorausgehen, so an einander reihet, dass das Ohr durch die ihnen mangelnde Betonung auf eine zu erwartende aufmerksam wird.

segments.label: §66, de source block5
segments.text: Dagegen schafft der Accent verschiedene Tongebiete und trennt die Sylben, indem er eine neue Betonung anheben lässt.

segments.label: §66, de source block6
segments.text: Er folgt hierin unmittelbar der Richtung des Gedanken, und dient, den Fluss der Rede dem Fluss der Gedanken ähnlich zu machen, aber er wird bedingt durch die Gesetze der Aussprache, und fügt sich, jedoch mehr oder weniger, denen des Wohllauts.

segments.label: §66, de source block7
segments.text: Man darf aber den Accent in diesem Sinne nicht mit andren Lautveränderungen der Vocale verwechseln, die wohl auch durch Accentzeichen angedeutet werden, und auch in Hebung oder Senkung der Stimme bestehen.

segments.label: §66, de source block8
segments.text: Diese sind nur bestimmt durch Verschiedenheit der Intonation eine grössere Anzahl von Lauten möglich zu machen, als die intonationfreie Beschaffenheit derselben herzugeben vermag.

segments.label: §66, de source block9
segments.text: Dies ist der Fall mit den Chinesischen Accentzeichen, da es im Chinesischen eigentlich so viele Abarten jedes Vocals giebt, als der Vocal Intonationen annehmen kann.

segments.label: §66, de source block10
segments.text: Denn im Grunde fällt die Intonation der Sylbe doch immer nur auf den Vocal.

segments.label: §66, de source block11
segments.text: Durch diese Intonationen vermehrt sich mithin der Umfang des Alphabets.

segments.label: §66, codex source block1
segments.text: Just as temporal measure belongs for the most part to the peculiar nature of tones, so accent belongs exclusively to the speaker’s intention.

segments.label: §66, codex source block2
segments.text: It is the means through which language links and separates discourse, which without it would consist merely of fundamental parts strung together, into distinct coordinate and subordinate wholes.

segments.label: §66, codex source block3
segments.text: For by accentuating one syllable, accent makes the following syllables unaccented, thereby drawing them into the domain of the accented syllable and thus joining them to it.

segments.label: §66, codex source block4
segments.text: The same happens when syllables preceding the accentuation are strung together in such a way that their lack of accentuation alerts the ear to an accentuation to be expected.

segments.label: §66, codex source block5
segments.text: Conversely, accent creates different domains of tone and separates syllables by allowing a new accentuation to begin.

segments.label: §66, codex source block6
segments.text: In this it follows the direction of thought immediately, and serves to make the flow of discourse resemble the flow of thoughts; but it is conditioned by the laws of pronunciation and conforms, though to a greater or lesser degree, to those of euphony.

segments.label: §66, codex source block7
segments.text: Accent in this sense must not, however, be confused with other changes in the sound of vowels, which may likewise be indicated by accent marks and likewise consist in raising or lowering the voice.

segments.label: §66, codex source block8
segments.text: These are intended only to make possible, through differences of intonation, a greater number of sounds than their character without intonation can provide.

segments.label: §66, codex source block9
segments.text: This is the case with Chinese accent marks, since in Chinese there are, properly speaking, as many varieties of each vowel as the vowel can assume intonations.

segments.label: §66, codex source block10
segments.text: For fundamentally the intonation of the syllable always falls on the vowel alone.

segments.label: §66, codex source block11
segments.text: Through these intonations, therefore, the range of the alphabet increases.

segments.label: §66, muse source block1
segments.text: Just as time-measure belongs for the most part to the peculiar nature of the tones, so accent belongs exclusively to the speaker's intention.

segments.label: §66, muse source block2
segments.text: It is the means by which language connects and separates speech, which without it would consist of fundamental parts merely strung together, into different co-ordinate and subordinate wholes.

segments.label: §66, muse source block3
segments.text: For by accentuating a syllable, accent makes the following syllables toneless, thus draws them into the domain of the accentuated one, and consequently connects them with it.

segments.label: §66, muse source block4
segments.text: The same happens when one strings together syllables preceding the accentuation in such a way that the ear, through the accentuation they lack, is made attentive to one to be expected.

segments.label: §66, muse source block5
segments.text: On the other hand, accent creates different tone-domains and separates the syllables by letting a new accentuation begin.

segments.label: §66, muse source block6
segments.text: In this it follows immediately the direction of thought and serves to make the flow of speech like the flow of thoughts, but it is conditioned by the laws of pronunciation and submits, though more or less, to those of euphony.

segments.label: §66, muse source block7
segments.text: But accent in this sense must not be confused with other sound-changes of the vowels, which may indeed also be indicated by accent signs and also consist in raising or lowering of the voice.

segments.label: §66, muse source block8
segments.text: These are intended only to make possible, through difference of intonation, a greater number of sounds than the character of those sounds, free of intonation, can yield.

segments.label: §66, muse source block9
segments.text: This is the case with the Chinese accent signs, since in Chinese there are properly as many varieties of each vowel as the vowel can assume intonations.

segments.label: §66, muse source block10
segments.text: For fundamentally the intonation of the syllable always falls only on the vowel after all.

segments.label: §66, muse source block11
segments.text: Through these intonations, consequently, the extent of the alphabet increases.

segments.label: §66, astra source block1
segments.text: Just as quantity belongs for the most part to the particular nature of sounds, so accent belongs exclusively to the speaker’s intention.

segments.label: §66, astra source block2
segments.text: It is the means by which language joins and divides speech into different coordinate and subordinate wholes; without it, speech would consist merely of basic parts strung together.

segments.label: §66, astra source block3
segments.text: For by accenting one syllable, accent makes those that follow unaccented, thereby drawing them into the domain of the accented syllable and thus joining them to it.

segments.label: §66, astra source block4
segments.text: The same thing happens when syllables preceding the accent are strung together in such a way that their lack of accent alerts the ear to an accent still to come.

segments.label: §66, astra source block5
segments.text: Conversely, accent creates different domains of sound and separates the syllables by initiating a new accentuation.

segments.label: §66, astra source block6
segments.text: Here it follows the direction of thought immediately and serves to make the flow of speech resemble the flow of thoughts; but it is conditioned by the laws of pronunciation and submits, though to a greater or lesser degree, to those of euphony.

segments.label: §66, astra source block7
segments.text: Accent in this sense must not, however, be confused with other changes in vowel sounds that are likewise indicated by accent marks and likewise consist in raising or lowering the voice.

segments.label: §66, astra source block8
segments.text: These are intended only to make possible, through differences of intonation, a greater number of sounds than the nature of those sounds without intonation can yield.

segments.label: §66, astra source block9
segments.text: This is the case with Chinese accent marks, since in Chinese there are, properly speaking, as many varieties of each vowel as there are intonations the vowel can take.

segments.label: §66, astra source block10
segments.text: For at bottom, the intonation of a syllable always falls only on its vowel.

segments.label: §66, astra source block11
segments.text: These intonations thus increase the range of the alphabet.

segments.label: §67, de source block1
segments.text: Die wichtigste Art des wahren Accents und diejenige, welche am meisten der Sprache angehört, ist der Wortaccent.

segments.label: §67, de source block2
segments.text: Der Redeaccent wechselt natürlich nach der Beschaffenheit der Rede und kann nicht an den Theilen der unverbundenen Sprache haften.

segments.label: §67, de source block3
segments.text: Aber seine Behandlung im Ganzen gehört allerdings zu der Natur der Sprache.

segments.label: §67, de source block4
segments.text: Sie liegt zwar in der der Nation eigenthümlichen Vorstellungs- und Empfindungsweise, allein die Sprache kann von dieser auch niemals getrennt werden, und besteht, ausser den gleichsam todten Elementen, immer zugleich aus der in der Seele der Redenden liegenden Eigenthümlichkeit des lebendigen Vortrags, nur dass sich dieser an todten Sprachen gar nicht, oder wenigstens nur unvollkommen erkennen lässt.

segments.label: §67, de source block5
segments.text: In der Sanskrita Sprache fehlen bis jetzt alle Nachrichten über die Accentuation, und wenn die der Griechischen sich auch in ihren Zeichen erhalten hat, so bleiben über die Art des lebendigen wirklichen Vortrags der Accente in Verbindung einerseits mit dem Redeaccent, andrerseits mit dem Zeitmass noch viele Zweifel übrig.

segments.label: §67, codex source block1
segments.text: The most important kind of true accent, and the one that belongs most fully to language, is word accent.

segments.label: §67, codex source block2
segments.text: Discourse accent naturally varies with the character of the discourse and cannot adhere to the parts of language outside their connection in discourse.

segments.label: §67, codex source block3
segments.text: But its treatment as a whole certainly belongs to the nature of the language.

segments.label: §67, codex source block4
segments.text: This treatment admittedly lies in the nation’s distinctive way of representing things and feeling, but language can never be separated from this either, and, besides its as it were dead elements, always consists also in the distinctive character of living delivery that lies in the souls of its speakers; only, in dead languages this delivery cannot be discerned at all, or at least only imperfectly.

segments.label: §67, codex source block5
segments.text: For Sanskrit, all information about accentuation is so far lacking; and although Greek accentuation has been preserved in its signs, many doubts remain about the manner of the living, actual delivery of the accents in conjunction with discourse accent on the one hand and temporal measure on the other.

segments.label: §67, muse source block1
segments.text: The most important kind of true accent, and the one that belongs most to language, is word-accent.

segments.label: §67, muse source block2
segments.text: Speech-accent naturally changes according to the character of the speech and cannot adhere to the parts of unconnected language.

segments.label: §67, muse source block3
segments.text: But its treatment as a whole does belong to the nature of language.

segments.label: §67, muse source block4
segments.text: It lies, indeed, in the nation's peculiar manner of representation and feeling, but language can also never be separated from this, and, apart from the as it were dead elements, always consists at the same time of the peculiarity of living delivery lying in the soul of the speakers, except that in dead languages this cannot be recognized at all, or at least only imperfectly.

segments.label: §67, muse source block5
segments.text: In the Sanskrit language all information about accentuation is so far lacking, and even if that of Greek has been preserved in its signs, many doubts still remain about the manner of the living, actual delivery of the accents in combination on the one hand with speech-accent, on the other with time-measure.
