evidence.excerpt: The claim of exclusive dependence on intention is Humboldt’s. He immediately adds constraints from pronunciation and euphony, and in 67 treats word accent as belonging to the language; it should not be paraphrased as free choice of the accent on each word.
evidence.statement: Keep the absolute assertion and its later constraints visible.

evidence.excerpt: Deleted after ‘syllable’: ‘or a word’.
evidence.statement: Translate the complete printed source note, retaining authorship and original callout metadata. The English callout is at the corresponding phrase or nearest readable boundary; it does not restore a reported deletion into the text.

evidence.excerpt: Tone is not confined to vowels in all Chinese varieties. Cantonese has tone-bearing syllabic nasals, such as *m4* “no” and *ng5* “five”, with no vowel; see [Hong Kong Polytechnic University, “Understanding Finals”](https://www.polyu.edu.hk/clc/cantonese/phoneticKnowledge/vowel/recognizingVowel/?lang=en), the syllabic-nasals table. This does not identify the exact varieties covered by Humboldt’s sources.
evidence.statement: Qualify the vowel-only generalization with copied, source-checked examples.

evidence.excerpt: In Chinese grammars, the intonations are admittedly called modifications of the words, or, what there amounts to the same thing, of the syllables, which is indeed much more appropriate in those grammars. Yet, properly speaking, they rest only on the vowel ending; hence, speaking in the manner of other languages, it is more natural to say that each simple and compound vowel ending can have such and such an intonation, and that the words then take the vowel ending intoned in this or that way according to differences in their meaning. In this way the matter is put on the same footing as the short and long vowels of other languages.
evidence.statement: Translate the complete printed source note, retaining authorship and original callout metadata. The English callout is at the corresponding phrase or nearest readable boundary; it does not restore a reported deletion into the text.

evidence.excerpt: This records the limits of Humboldt’s information, not a present absence of evidence. Later descriptions document accent marks in Vedic texts; see [Whitney, Sanskrit Grammar, §87](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Sanskrit_Grammar_(Whitney)/Chapter_II). Written notation does not by itself recover every detail of spoken delivery.
evidence.statement: Distinguish historical knowledge and the evidential limits of notation.

evidence.excerpt: The argument links unity of concept with unity of accent. Compare 69, where Humboldt considers several words joining as one accentual group; a group heard as one whole need not simply be one independent word.
evidence.statement: Expose the relation between the ideal word-unity argument and the later enclitic qualification.

evidence.excerpt: “When they do combine” makes explicit the reading that conceptual union requires one element to predominate. The final “in that case” in the German could instead be attached to the preceding negative alternative; its reference is not explicit.
evidence.statement: Expose the interpretive scope of alsdann rather than hide it in the apparatus.

evidence.excerpt: The Sanskrit pronouns of the first and second persons do have, for certain cases, a second, more frequently used, abbreviated form alongside the full form, whose fullness is due to its less frequent use. But it does not appear that this second form was used exclusively as an enclitic.
evidence.statement: Translate the complete printed source note, retaining authorship and original callout metadata. The English callout is at the corresponding phrase or nearest readable boundary; it does not restore a reported deletion into the text.

evidence.excerpt: A “letter” often means a speech-sound element, and “alphabet” the inventory or system of such sounds. They are not automatically written characters or a modern phoneme inventory. Where writing enters in 62 and 71, written signs are identified separately; Buchstabenschrift is alphabetic writing.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Ton and Laut overlap as “sound”; articulated sound is shaped to carry thought. Geräusch is the accompanying noise Humboldt wants removed, though his evaluation of particular consonants is qualified in the note on 57. Schall in 71 is the transient acoustic occurrence to which the written sign recalls us.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: These are “mind”, “understanding” and “soul” in this unit. The English keeps the recurring German terms recoverable without turning every lexical difference into a separate modern psychological mechanism. Understanding here names an intellectual capacity, not just successful comprehension of an utterance.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Here the term concerns language’s intellectual character and its relation to thought. The earlier division used “intellectual life” where the bearer was a nation and its orientation; that contextual change does not establish different faculties. “Intellectual cultivation” in 70 renders a different expression, intellectuelle Bildung.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: The German uses several overlapping expressions for alterations of speech sounds. The contexts include inflection, changes inside words and changes when words meet; these are not automatically historical sound laws or merely spelling changes. The German forms remain available in the linked record.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Words can be linked by changes at their boundaries and by contraction. Humboldt distinguishes changes joining parts of one word from those joining otherwise independent words, criticizes the latter for obscuring conceptual divisions, and allows a poetic advantage. This is his argument, not a modern rule for counting words.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Quantity concerns timing, including long and short vowels and syllabic duration; it is distinct from accent. Consonants also enter the argument in 65, so syllabic timing should not be reduced to vowel length alone. Rhythm and accent can support or oppose one another in Humboldt’s account.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Accent organizes prominence and groups in speech; word accent belongs to the word, discourse accent varies with delivery. Intonation in the Chinese discussion concerns tone distinctions, not simply sentence melody. These historical categories overlap with modern stress, pitch accent and tone without being identical to them.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Here an enclitic word loses its independent accent and attaches to another word; an orthotonic form has its own accent. Humboldt’s point is that an independent word’s pronunciation and accent can change through attachment, which complicates the picture of one word as one audible whole.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: In the note on 64, a root is first “stamped” into a word and the word is then reshaped further by Taddhita suffixes. The metaphor distinguishes stages of formation; the note warns that the rules loosely called “internal” do not apply uniformly at every stage.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Euphony means pleasing sound as assessed in the argument. Roughness, purity and refinement are Humboldt’s aesthetic and developmental evaluations; they are not measurements of a people’s intellectual capacities. Keep the sensory description distinct from the value attached to it.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

evidence.excerpt: Geltung varies with its bearer: the conceptual force of language, the sway of quantity, a word’s independent standing, or its significance for the understanding. Lautgeltung concerns audible realization. These are related contributions or kinds of standing, not uniformly logical validity.
evidence.statement: Recurring local terminology guide, not a universal fixed equivalence.

text_version.body: Der Einfluss des Lautsystems erstreckt sich über die ganze Sprache, und ein sorgfältiges Studium aller Eigenthümlichkeiten desselben ist die Grundlage jeder genauen Sprachuntersuchung. Ohne die vollständige Kenntniss der Lautbehandlung, der Verhältnisse und Verwandtschaft der Buchstaben, die in jeder Sprache andren Gesetzen und Gewohnheiten unterliegen, bleibt die Erklärung der grammatischen Formen und das Eingehen in das Ganze des Sprachsystems allemal mangelhaft. (29.) Unmittelbar beruht auf dem Lautsystem die Verständlichkeit, der Nachdruck und der Wohllaut der Rede, es wirkt aber zugleich auf die reine und feine Intellectualitaet der Sprache, und hierin ist seine Wichtigkeit bisher vielleicht nicht hinlänglich gewürdigt worden. Sie leuchtet aber sogleich ein, als man sich daran erinnert, dass (21.) der ganze Begriff der Sprache in dem des articulirten Lautes liegt, und dass die Art, wie jede Sprache diesen Begriff auffasst, sich in ihrem Alphabet, als dem System ihrer articulirten Laute darstellt.

text_version.body: The influence of the sound system extends throughout language, and a careful study of all its peculiarities is the foundation of every exact investigation of language. Without a complete knowledge of the treatment of sounds and of the relations and affinities of letters, which are subject to different laws and habits in every language, the explanation of grammatical forms and the exploration of the linguistic system as a whole always remain deficient. (29.) The intelligibility, force and euphony of discourse depend directly on the sound system, but it also affects the pure and refined intellectuality of language, and in this respect its importance has perhaps not yet been adequately appreciated. Yet this importance becomes immediately apparent when we recall that (21.) the whole concept of language lies in that of articulated sound, and that each language’s way of apprehending this concept is manifested in its alphabet, as the system of its articulated sounds.

text_version.body: Das erste ist die Absonderung des Tones von allem mitschallendem Geräusch, welche ihn auf einen wahren Sprachlaut zurückführt. Er soll nur den Begriff anregen, aus dem er entspringt, und darf nicht mehr Körper besitzen, als dazu erforderlich ist. Gerade mit dem wenigsten tritt das Charakteristische am schärfsten hervor. Indem der Geist den thierischen Laut durchdringt, wird dieser zum articulirten, verliert aber nicht in allen Sprachen (28.) seine ursprüngliche Natur ganz und rein, sondern mischt den Tönen ein Schnalzen, Schmettern, Zischen, Schnarren oder Hauchen bei, was man in einigen, vorzüglich Afrikanischen Sprachen in grosser Rohheit, aber in feineren Spuren auch in hoch ausgebildeten antrifft. Stumpfheit des geistigen Sprachdranges und physische Rauhigkeit der Organe mögen in solchen Fällen zusammenwirken, aber Geist und Organe verfeinern sich durch gegenseitige Einwirkung auf einander, und die Rauhigkeit der Töne schleift sich daher oft in der Fortbildung der Sprachen durch die Zeit allmählich ab.

text_version.body: The first step is to separate the tone from all accompanying noise, thereby reducing it to a true speech sound. It should evoke only the concept from which it springs, and must possess no more body than is required for this. It is precisely with the least body that its distinctive character emerges most sharply. As the mind penetrates the animal sound, the latter becomes articulated; but not in every language (28.) does it wholly and purely lose its original nature: instead, it mingles the tones with clicking, blaring, hissing, rasping or breathing, which we encounter in great crudity in some languages, especially African ones, but also in finer traces in highly developed languages. Dullness of the mind’s impulse towards language and physical roughness of the organs may act together in such cases; but mind and organs refine one another through their mutual influence, and the roughness of the tones is therefore often gradually worn away over time as languages develop.

text_version.body: Allein auch die wirklichen, von mitschallendem Geräusch gereinigten Sprachlaute müssen bestimmt von einander geschieden seyn, nicht einer in den andren hinübertönen. Die Buchstaben liegen nicht gleichsam bestimmt geschieden in den Sprachwerkzeugen. Man muss sich vielmehr die Bewegung derselben, welche einer bestimmten Gattung das Daseyn giebt, als ein Continuum denken, wo in jedem Punkte durch plötzliche Fixirung der Laut eine um ein wenig verschiedene Beschaffenheit erhalten würde, je nachdem z. B. die Lippen sich mehr oder weniger öffnen, die Zunge schneller oder langsamer, fester oder leiser, mit schmalerer oder breiterer Fläche anschlägt u. s. f. Jeder Laut hat mithin eine eigne Sphäre, in welcher er einen bestimmten, aber bei weitem nicht den einzig möglichen Punkt einnimmt. Diesen Punkt weist ihm die sich bildende Gewohnheit der Nation an, so entsteht ihr besondres Alphabet, und über dieser Entstehung kann Glück und Misgeschick walten.

text_version.body: But even genuine speech sounds, purified of accompanying noise, must be distinctly separated from one another, rather than letting one shade audibly into another. Letters do not lie, as it were, distinctly separated in the organs of speech. Rather, we must conceive the movement of these organs that brings a particular kind of sound into being as a continuum, at any point in which a sudden fixing would give the sound a slightly different character, according, for example, to whether the lips open more or less, the tongue strikes more quickly or slowly, more firmly or gently, with a narrower or broader surface, and so forth. Every sound thus has a sphere of its own, within which it occupies a definite point, though by no means the only possible one. The developing habit of the nation assigns it this point; this is how the nation’s particular alphabet arises, and good or ill fortune may preside over its emergence.

text_version.body: But even the real speech sounds, purified of accompanying noise, must be definitely separated from one another; one must not sound over into another. The letters do not lie, as it were, definitely separated in the organs of speech. Rather, one must think of their movement, which gives existence to a definite kind, as a continuum in which at every point, by sudden fixation, the sound would receive a character differing by a little, according as, for example, the lips open more or less, the tongue strikes more quickly or more slowly, more firmly or more softly, with a narrower or broader surface, and so on. Every sound thus has its own sphere, in which it occupies a definite point, but by far not the only possible one. The nation's habit, as it forms itself, assigns this point to it; in this way its particular alphabet arises, and fortune and misfortune can hold sway over this arising.

text_version.body: Der Einfluss mangelnder reiner Geschiedenheit der Töne wirkt aber noch weit über die blosse Gefahr des Misverständnisses hinaus. Der articulirte Laut ist zu enge mit dem Geiste verschwistert, als dass nicht seine richtige und fehlerhafte Bildung immer wieder einen entsprechenden Einfluss auf denselben ausüben, dass dieser sich nicht wieder auch in der Rückwirkung des Geistes zeigen, und auf diese Weise nicht eine bis ins Unendliche fortgehende Wechselwirkung entstehen sollte, in welche der Geist zwar seine reinere Natur immer siegend hineinträgt, aber in diesem Uebergewicht immer wieder in etwas durch den widerstrebenden Stoff gehemmt wird. Reine Bestimmtheit, glückliche Klarheit, eindringende Schärfe der Begriffe in einer Nation hängen daher gar sehr von der reinen Geschiedenheit der Grundlaute ihres Alphabetes ab.

text_version.body: The influence of a lack of clear separation between tones, however, extends far beyond the mere danger of misunderstanding. Articulated sound is too closely akin to the mind for its correct or faulty formation not to exert a corresponding influence on the mind in turn, for this influence not to manifest itself again in the mind’s reaction, and for an interaction continuing to infinity not to arise in this way: into this interaction the mind always brings its purer nature victoriously, yet even in its ascendancy it is repeatedly checked to some degree by the resistant material. The pure definiteness, felicitous clarity and penetrating sharpness of a nation’s concepts therefore depend very greatly on the clear separation of the fundamental sounds of its alphabet.

text_version.body: Es giebt, auch im Gebrauche der blossen articulirten Laute, ohne alle musikalische oder dichterische Beziehung, ein aesthetisches Gefühl, durch das eine Nation getrieben wird, jeden, ihm sein volles Recht einräumend, ganz und hell austönen zu lassen, indem eine andre, welcher dies Gefühl mangelt, oder die dasselbe andren Rücksichten, wie im Englischen der Gewalt des Accents, unterordnet, viele verschluckt, verschmilzt oder verdunkelt. Hiervon lässt sich in Rücksicht auf die Begriffe dasselbe, als von dem Mangel an richtiger Geschiedenheit sagen. Es kommt alsdann darauf an, wie dasjenige, was den Begriffen dadurch an ruhig leuchtender Klarheit entgeht, auf andre Weise ersetzt wird.

text_version.body: Even in the use of articulated sounds alone, without any musical or poetic reference, there is an aesthetic feeling that impels one nation to allow each sound its full due and let it ring out fully and brightly, whereas another nation, which lacks this feeling or subordinates it to other considerations, as in English to the power of accent, swallows, merges or obscures many sounds. With regard to concepts, the same may be said of this as of the lack of proper separation. The question then is how the calmly shining clarity thereby lost to concepts is made good in other ways.

text_version.body: Durch den Gebrauch der Sprache entsteht, und zwar in dem Grade mehr, in welchem irgend eine ein glücklich gewähltes Lautsystem richtig anwendet, im Geiste Sinn für feine Lautunterscheidung und Wohlgefallen daran. Da nun die Rede auch vieler Unterscheidungen bedarf, um die Begriffe in allen ihren Verhältnissen und Schattirungen auszudrücken und anzuregen, so kommt jener Sinn diesem Bedürfniss sehr glücklich zu Statten. Denn es geht nun Neigung und Fähigkeit hervor, diese Unterschiede durch einzelne Buchstabenveränderung zu bezeichnen, und an ihr zu erkennen, worin der Ursprung aller Inflexion liegt, man mag sie nun für gleichzeitig mit der Sprache, oder für später in ihr entstanden halten. Es wird aber durch sie der doppelte Vorzug gewonnen, der Idee nur gerade soviel Körper zu geben, als sie bedarf, und durch den in sich selbst ganz bedeutungslosen Buchstaben, jeden irre leitenden Nebenbegriff zu vermeiden. Es liegt in der Sprache ein durch alle ihre Functionen gehendes und sich immer steigerndes Streben nach Läuterung der Intellectualität. So wie sie (57.) von dem Sprachlaut das mitschallende Geräusch absondert, so entfernt sie auch in dem durch Sprache Gedachten die Vorstellung jedes nicht durch den Gedanken nothwendig werdenden Stoffs, und verdrängt ihn da, wo er als Zeichen der Form auftreten will, durch den bedeutungslosen Laut. Es ist daher eine Eigenschaft aller für den Geist angemessner gebildeten Sprachen, wenn man sie mit andren, ihnen darin entgegengesetzten vergleicht, eine geringere Masse des Stoffes bei dem Ausdruck derselben Idee anzuregen, und diese dadurch freier und geläuterter hervortreten zu lassen.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §61 — checked German

text_version.body: The use of language produces in the mind a sense for fine distinctions of sound and a pleasure in them, and does so to a greater degree the more correctly a language employs a well-chosen sound system. Since discourse also needs many distinctions in order to express and evoke concepts in all their relations and shades, this sense serves that need most happily. For there now arise an inclination and an ability to mark these differences through changes of individual letters and to recognise them by those changes; in this lies the origin of all inflection, whether we regard it as arising simultaneously with language or later within it. Through inflection, however, a double advantage is gained: the idea is given only just as much body as it requires, and the letter, which is entirely meaningless in itself, avoids every misleading subsidiary concept. There is in language a striving towards the purification of intellectuality that runs through all its functions and continually intensifies. Just as language (57.) separates accompanying noise from the speech sound, so too, in what is thought through language, it removes the representation of any material not made necessary by the thought, and wherever such material seeks to appear as a sign of form, it displaces it with meaningless sound. It is therefore a property of all languages more suitably formed for the mind, when compared with others opposed to them in this respect, to evoke a smaller mass of material in expressing the same idea, and thereby to let the idea emerge more freely and in greater purity.

text_version.body: Through the use of language there arises in the mind, and indeed to a greater degree in proportion as any language rightly applies a happily chosen sound system, a sense for fine discrimination of sounds and pleasure in it. Now, since speech also needs many distinctions in order to express and arouse concepts in all their relations and shadings, that sense comes very happily to the aid of this need. For there now proceeds from it an inclination and ability to designate these differences by change of a single letter and to recognize them by it, in which lies the origin of all inflexion, whether one regards it as simultaneous with language or as having arisen later in it. But through it the double advantage is gained of giving the idea only just as much body as it needs, and, through the letter, in itself quite meaningless, of avoiding every misleading subsidiary concept. There lies in language a striving after purification of intellectuality, proceeding through all its functions and ever increasing. Just as it (57.) separates the accompanying noise from the speech sound, so also in what is thought through language it removes the representation of every material not made necessary by the thought, and displaces it, where it wants to appear as a sign of form, by the meaningless sound. It is therefore a property of all languages formed more appropriately for the mind, when one compares them with others opposite to them in this respect, to arouse a smaller mass of material in the expression of the same idea, and thereby to let the latter emerge more freely and in a more purified form.

text_version.body: Es ist eine natürliche und fast nothwendige Folge der reinen Scheidung der Töne, dass das Alphabet dadurch mehr Umfang erhält. Denn die Töne, welche das Ohr bei dunkler, unausgebildeter Aussprache leicht verwechseln konnte, treten nun bestimmt aus einander. Bisweilen entsteht aber auch die Verschiedenheit des Umfanges des Alphabets aus besondren Lauteigenthümlichkeiten und Gewohnheiten der Nationen, durch welche demselben einzelne Buchstaben, wie das gestrichene Polnische l, und sogar ganze Classen derselben, wie die Indischen Cerebralen oder Lingualen zuwachsen. Die Lage und Bewegung der Sprachwerkzeuge, und das Fallen der einzelnen Töne in dieselben oder verschiedene Sphären (58.) macht, dass die Buchstaben in gegenseitigen Beziehungen und Verhältnissen zu einander stehn, und in dem Alphabet ein mehr oder minder vollständiges System von Tönen entdeckt werden kann. Nach einmal entstandener Schrift und bei hinzutretender grammatischer Behandlung kann ein Alphabet in dieser Beziehung ein fester bestimmtes und feiner ausgebildetes System erhalten, als ursprünglich in dem Sprachgebrauch der Nation lag, und so mag es dem Sanskrita Alphabet, dessen Typus sich über die noch lebenden Sprachen eines grossen Theils von Süd-Asien verbreitet hat, ergangen seyn. Allein der Totalitaet nach liegt ein solches System immer in den Sprachanlagen und Sprachgewohnheiten der Nationen, und die Bestimmtheit, welche es allerdings durch glücklich gewählte Schriftzeichen gewinnt, wirkt wieder auf das Sprechen zurück, und verwandelt sich in ihr wahres Eigenthum.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §62 — checked German

text_version.body: It is a natural and almost necessary consequence of the clear separation of tones that the alphabet thereby gains in range. For tones that the ear could easily confuse in obscure, undeveloped pronunciation now stand distinctly apart. Sometimes, however, differences in the range of the alphabet also arise from nations’ particular peculiarities and habits of sound, through which individual letters, such as the Polish l with a stroke, and even whole classes of letters, such as the Indian cerebrals or linguals, are added to it. The position and movement of the organs of speech, and the fact that individual tones fall within the same or different spheres (58.), mean that letters stand in mutual relations and proportions, and that a more or less complete system of tones can be discovered in the alphabet. Once writing has arisen and grammatical treatment is added, an alphabet can acquire in this respect a more firmly determined and more finely developed system than originally existed in the nation’s linguistic usage; this may have happened to the Sanskrit alphabet, whose pattern has spread across the still living languages of a large part of southern Asia. Yet in its totality such a system always lies in nations’ linguistic dispositions and habits, and the definiteness it admittedly gains through well-chosen written signs acts back upon speaking and becomes the nations’ true possession.

text_version.body: It is a natural and almost necessary consequence of the pure separation of the tones that the alphabet thereby receives greater extent. For the tones which the ear could easily confuse in obscure, undeveloped pronunciation now step definitely apart from one another. Sometimes, however, the difference in the extent of the alphabet also arises from particular sound peculiarities and habits of nations, by which single letters, such as the barred Polish l, and even whole classes of them, such as the Indian cerebrals or linguals, accrue to it. The position and movement of the organs of speech, and the falling of the individual tones into the same or different spheres (58.), cause the letters to stand in reciprocal connections and relations to one another, and allow a more or less complete system of tones to be discovered in the alphabet. After writing has once arisen, and with grammatical treatment added, an alphabet can in this respect receive a more firmly definite and more finely developed system than originally lay in the nation's linguistic usage, and this may have been the case with the Sanskrit alphabet, whose type has spread over the still living languages of a great part of southern Asia. But as a totality such a system always lies in the nations' dispositions and habits for language, and the definiteness which it admittedly gains through happily chosen written characters reacts in turn upon speaking and is transformed into their true property.

Once writing has come into being, and grammatical study has been added to it, an alphabet can acquire in this respect a more firmly defined and finely developed system than was originally present in the nation’s language use. This may have happened to the Sanskrit alphabet, whose pattern has spread to the languages still living in a large part of South Asia. Yet in its totality such a system always lies in nations’ linguistic dispositions and habits, and the definiteness it admittedly gains through well-chosen written signs acts back upon speaking and becomes the nations’ true possession.

text_version.body: Bei der Verbindung mehrerer Buchstaben zur Sylbe zeigen sich neue Eigenthümlichkeiten des Lautsystems, je nachdem die Sprachen das Zusammentreffen einiger Buchstaben begünstigen, andrer vermeiden, und eine Anzahl von Sylben ausstossen. Man hat daher, ausser dem Umfange des Alphabets, auch auf den der durch dasselbe möglichen Sylben zu achten. Es ist bemerkenswerth, dass gerade die Sprachen der Wilden, die man wohl der Rauhigkeit zu beschuldigen pflegt, viele Sylben ausstossen, die in hochgebildeten Sprachen geduldet werden. Es mag dies zum Theil aus der schon im Vorigen bemerkten reizbareren Empfindlichkeit der Sinne dieser Völker, und zum Theil daraus herrühren, dass die gebildetere Sprache oft Sylben zusammenzieht, wo die ursprünglichere jede für sich auf einander folgen lässt.

text_version.body: When several letters are combined into a syllable, new peculiarities of the sound system become apparent, according to whether languages favour the coming together of certain letters, avoid that of others, and exclude a number of syllables. Besides the range of the alphabet, we must therefore also attend to the range of syllables possible through it. It is remarkable that precisely the languages of savages, which people are apt to accuse of roughness, exclude many syllables tolerated in highly cultivated languages. This may arise partly from the more readily excited sensitivity of these peoples’ senses, already noted above, and partly from the fact that the more cultivated language often contracts syllables where the more original language lets each follow separately in succession.

text_version.body: In diesen Systemen liegen die Gründe und die Bedingungen der Buchstabenveränderung, die gleichfalls nur zum Theil durch die allgemeinere Natur der Sprachwerkzeuge gegeben ist, ausserdem aber auf den besondren Lautgewohnheiten jedes Volkes beruht. Denn wenn die Natur der Buchstaben auch die Art der Verwandlung bestimmt, so hängt es von dem Ohr und den Sprachwerkzeugen jedes Volkes ab, wie empfindlich es für diesen gegenseitigen Einfluss der Laute auf einander bei ihrer Berührung ist. Je näher sich in einem sehr systematischen Alphabet von bedeutendem Umfange die Töne stehen, und je klarer und bestimmter in einem solchen ihr Verhältniss erkannt wird, desto mehr wächst die Neigung zur Buchstabenverwandlung, so wie hinwiederum sie gar sehr zur feineren Lautunterscheidung und zur Systematisirung des Alphabets beiträgt. Man könnte glauben, dass das Ohr uncultivirter Nationen diese Feinheiten der Töne überhörte und vernachlässigte, man findet aber gerade bei ihnen sehr häufige Buchstabenverwandlungen, was den beiden Ursachen zuzuschreiben seyn mag, dass gerade die Sinne des der Natur näher stehenden Menschen eine schärfere Empfindlichkeit besitzen, und dass der Uncultivirte die Rede vor dem Verstände wie ein sich überall berührendes Continuum ansieht, indess der Gebildete auch in der fortlaufenden Rede das Verschleifen der Töne nach den Pausen des Verstandes durch die Zunge hemmt. Aber eine wahre Nationaleigenheit der Indischen Völker, für die sich kein weiterer Grund anführen lässt, ist wohl die so häufige Verkettung mehrerer Worte durch Buchstabenverwandlung und Zusammenziehung, von der es wenigstens nicht sichtbar ist, ob auch andre Nationen sie in dem Masse gekannt haben. Auf den ersten Anblick geräth man in Versuchung die mannigfaltigen im Sanskrit hieraus entstehenden Regeln wenigstens zum Theil der Systemsucht der Grammatiker zuzuschreiben. Allein diese Vermuthung verschwindet bei der Vergleichung der lebenden, aus dem Sanskrit hervorgegangenen Indischen Sprachen. Von der Telinga, in welcher diese Verkettung gerade vorzüglich häufig und schwierig zu erkennen ist, sagt Carey ausdrücklich, dass der Fremde, welcher dieselbe vernachlässigen wollte, gar nicht würde von den Eingebornen verstanden werden. Im Bengalischen dagegen wird sie nicht immer streng beobachtet, so dass man daraus noch deutlicher sieht, wie dieser Punkt von den individuellen Gewohnheiten der Stämme abhängt.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §63 — checked German

text_version.body: In these systems lie the grounds and conditions of letter change, which likewise is determined only in part by the more general nature of the organs of speech, but otherwise rests on each people’s particular habits of sound. For although the nature of the letters determines the kind of transformation, how sensitive a people is to this mutual influence of sounds upon one another when they come into contact depends on its ear and organs of speech. The closer the tones stand to one another in a highly systematic alphabet of considerable range, and the more clearly and distinctly their relationship is recognised in such an alphabet, the more the inclination towards letter transformation grows; conversely, this transformation contributes very greatly to finer distinctions of sound and to the systematisation of the alphabet. One might think that the ear of uncultivated nations would fail to hear and would neglect these subtleties of tone; yet it is precisely among them that very frequent letter transformations are found, which may be attributed to two causes: the senses of human beings closer to nature possess a keener sensitivity, and the uncultivated person regards discourse, before the understanding intervenes, as a continuum whose parts are everywhere in contact, whereas the cultivated person uses the tongue, even in continuous discourse, to check the running together of tones in accordance with the pauses of the understanding. But the very frequent chaining together of several words through letter transformation and contraction is probably a true national peculiarity of the Indian peoples, for which no further ground can be given; at least, it is not evident whether other nations too have known it to the same extent. At first sight one is tempted to attribute the manifold rules arising from this in Sanskrit, at least in part, to the grammarians’ passion for systems. But this conjecture disappears when one compares the living Indian languages that have emerged from Sanskrit. Of Telinga, in which this chaining is particularly frequent and difficult to recognise, Carey expressly says that a foreigner who chose to neglect it would not be understood by the native inhabitants at all. In Bengali, by contrast, it is not always strictly observed, making it still clearer how this point depends on the individual habits of the tribes.

But a true national peculiarity of the Indian peoples, for which no further ground can be adduced, is probably the so frequent chaining together of several words by letter-transformation and contraction, of which it is at least not visible whether other nations also have known it to the same degree. At first sight one is tempted to ascribe the manifold rules arising from this in Sanskrit at least in part to the grammarians' mania for system. Of Telinga, in which this chaining together is precisely especially frequent and difficult to recognize, Carey says expressly that a foreigner who wished to neglect it would not be understood by the natives at all. In Bengali, on the other hand, it is not always strictly observed, so that one sees from this still more clearly how this point depends on the individual habits of the tribes.

text_version.body: Den nächsten Einfluss hat diese Eigenthümlichkeit natürlich auf den Wohllaut. Es schmeichelt dem Ohre, wenn das harte Zusammentreffen widerstrebender und unharmonischer Laute möglichst vermieden wird. Aber die Wirkung erstreckt sich auch auf die ideale Geltung der Sprache, und die richtige Gliederung der Rede vor dem Verstände, dies jedoch nur dann, wenn die Buchstabenveränderung sich begnügt, Theile desselben Worts zu einem Ganzen zu verschmelzen, und nicht durch das Aneinanderreihen ganzer von einander unabhängiger Worte ein Ganzes vor dem Ohre bildet, das vor dem Verstände nicht, als solches, bestehen kann. Die letztere Gewohnheit kann ich nur insofern für nützlich halten, als sie in der Poesie ein Mittel mehr gewährt, die Worteinschnitte mit den rhythmischen in ein angemessenes Verhältniss zu bringen. Es entstehen nemlich dadurch andre, und häufiger grössere Lautganze, als die blosse Worteintheilung gewährt. Dagegen ist es für den Verstand und das Ohr störend, wenn sich der Endbuchstabe durch Veränderung da auf den ihm nachfolgenden vorbereitet, wo der Verstand logisch und das Ohr rhythmisch eine Pause verlangt. Beschränkt sich hingegen diese Lautverwandlung auf die Gränzen des Wortes, so wird sie zu einem phonetischen Mittel, die Rede in rein geschiedene Ganze zu zertheilen, und prägt dem Verstände auch sinnlich ein, dass das Element der Rede das Wort ist. Die logische Gliederung derselben erfährt keine Störung, sondern wird gelegentlich, so oft nemlich eine solche Lautveränderung eintritt, noch herausgehoben. Diesen Grundsatz der Nothwendigkeit, die Wortganze durch besondre Toneinheit zu charakterisiren, verkennt zwar auch die Sanskrita Sprache nicht, da in ihr andre Regeln für die Mitte der Wörter, als für das Zusammenstossen zweier gelten. Da aber diese Regeln in Einigem übereinkommen, und die für mehrere Worte auch für die Theile zusammengesetzter Wörter gelten, so erscheint die Wortabtheilung durch dies Mittel nicht in rein geschiedener sinnlicher Klarheit.

text_version.body: The most immediate influence of this peculiarity is naturally on euphony. It pleases the ear when the harsh collision of resistant and inharmonious sounds is avoided as far as possible. But the effect also extends to language’s efficacy in the realm of ideas and to the proper articulation of discourse for the understanding, though only when letter change confines itself to merging parts of the same word into a whole, rather than joining entire, mutually independent words in a sequence to form a whole for the ear that cannot subsist as such for the understanding. I can regard the latter habit as useful only in so far as, in poetry, it provides one more means of bringing word divisions into an appropriate relationship with rhythmic divisions. For it produces different, and more often larger, wholes of sound than division into words alone provides. By contrast, it disturbs both the understanding and the ear when a final letter prepares itself through change for the letter following it at a point where the understanding logically, and the ear rhythmically, demands a pause. If, however, this sound transformation confines itself within the boundaries of the word, it becomes a phonetic means of dividing discourse into clearly separated wholes, and impresses upon the understanding, through the senses too, that the element of discourse is the word. The logical articulation of discourse suffers no disturbance, but is occasionally given further prominence, namely whenever such a sound change occurs. Sanskrit, too, acknowledges this principle that word wholes must be characterised by a distinct unity of tone, since it has different rules for the interior of words and for the meeting of two words. But since these rules agree in some respects, and those for several words also apply to the parts of compound words, this means does not make word division manifest with clearly differentiated sensory clarity.

text_version.body: Das Zeitmass gehört den Sylben an. Da aber die Vocale die Sylbe bestimmen, und auch für sich allein bilden können, so wirkt das Gefühl für dieselbe auch auf die Vollständigkeit des Alphabets ein, in dem entweder alle Vocallaute, jeder in seiner Länge oder Kürze, rein geschieden vorkommen, oder nicht. Doch können die geschriebenen Zeichen nicht allein hierüber entscheiden. So bleibt es im Sanskrit immer zweifelhaft, ob die lebende Sprache nicht auch ein kurzes e und o besass. Das Zeitmass liegt ganz und gar in der Natur der Aussprache, und entzieht sich am meisten der willkührlichen Bestimmung. Selbst individuelle Anlagen und Gewohnheiten können einen geringeren Einfluss darauf ausüben, da z. B. das Zusammenstossen mehrerer Laute nothwendig mehr Zeit in der Aussprache erfordern muss. Dagegen kann Anlage, Gewohnheit und Absicht in einer Sprache die ganze Geltung des Zeitmasses in der Rede begünstigen, oder beschränken, und hieraus entspringt für den Wohllaut und die rhythmische Schönheit der Rede und der Sprache überhaupt, auch in ihrer Wirkung auf den Charakter, ein höchst wichtiger Unterschied. Der Ausdruck der Gedanken wird durch diese rhythmische Eigenthümlichkeit der Sprache weniger wesentlich betroffen. Zu grosse Begünstigung desselben kann ihm niemals nachtheilig werden, ungerechte Vernachlässigung nur insofern, als die nicht sorgfältige Scheidung der langen und kurzen Vocale denselben Nachtheil, als die Verdunkelung des reinen Lauts der Buchstaben überhaupt mit sich führt. Dagegen kann die Unterdrückung der natürlichen Geltung des Zeitmasses wohl den Gedankenausdruck zu einseitig herausheben. Denn Rhythmus und Accent stehen in einem Verhältniss zu einander, das da, wo nicht richtige Sprachbehandlung es in schönes Ebenmass ausgleicht, dem ersteren feindselig werden kann, indem es dem ruhigen Walten des Zeitmasses nicht immer gelingt, neben der Heftigkeit der Rede, oder dem scharf accentuirenden Verstände sein Recht zu behaupten. Das Vorherrschen des aesthetischen Gefühls, das aber ebensowohl in der Einseitigkeit, als der Rohheit Hindernisse finden kann, ist hier entscheidend, erhält seine Freiheit neben dem Nachdruck der Gedankenverbindung, und weist dem Accent selbst im Wort seine dem rhythmischen Wohllaut angemessene Stelle an.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §65 — checked German

text_version.body: Temporal measure belongs to syllables. But since vowels determine the syllable and can also form one by themselves, the feeling for the syllable also influences the completeness of the alphabet, in which either all vowel sounds occur clearly separated, each in its length or shortness, or they do not. Written signs alone, however, cannot decide this. Thus in Sanskrit it remains uncertain whether the living language did not also possess a short e and o. Temporal measure lies entirely in the nature of pronunciation and is least amenable to arbitrary determination. Even individual dispositions and habits can exert comparatively little influence on it, since, for example, the coming together of several sounds must necessarily require more time in pronunciation. By contrast, disposition, habit and intention in a language can favour or restrict the overall sway of temporal measure in discourse, and from this arises a difference of the greatest importance for the euphony and rhythmic beauty of discourse and of language generally, including its effect on character. The expression of thoughts is less essentially affected by this rhythmic peculiarity of language. Excessive favouring of temporal measure can never harm the expression of thoughts; undue neglect can do so only in so far as failure to distinguish long and short vowels carefully entails the same disadvantage as obscuring the pure sound of letters in general. By contrast, suppressing the natural sway of temporal measure may well give the expression of thought too one-sided a prominence. For rhythm and accent stand in a relationship that can become hostile to the former wherever proper treatment of language does not bring it into beautiful balance, since the calm sway of temporal measure does not always succeed in asserting its rights alongside the vehemence of discourse or the sharply accentuating understanding. The predominance of aesthetic feeling, which may, however, encounter obstacles in one-sidedness as well as in crudity, is decisive here: it preserves its freedom alongside the force of the connection of thoughts, and assigns even the accent within the word its place in accordance with rhythmic euphony.

text_version.body: Time-measure belongs to syllables. But since vowels determine the syllable and can also form it by themselves alone, the feeling for it also acts on the completeness of the alphabet, in that either all vowel sounds, each in its length or shortness, occur purely separated, or they do not. Yet the written signs cannot alone decide on this. Thus in Sanskrit it always remains doubtful whether the living language did not also possess a short e and o. Time-measure lies wholly in the nature of pronunciation, and withdraws itself most of all from arbitrary determination. Even individual dispositions and habits can exert only a lesser influence on it, since, for example, the coming together of several sounds must necessarily require more time in pronunciation. On the other hand, disposition, habit, and intention in a language can favour or restrict the whole validity of time-measure in speech, and from this there arises, for euphony and the rhythmical beauty of speech and of language in general, also in their effect on character, a most important difference. The expression of thoughts is less essentially affected by this rhythmical peculiarity of language. Too great favouring of it can never become detrimental to it; unjust neglect only in so far as the failure carefully to separate the long and short vowels brings with it the same disadvantage as the obscuring of the pure sound of the letters in general. On the other hand, suppression of the natural validity of time-measure may well throw the expression of thought into relief in too one-sided a way. For rhythm and accent stand in a relation to one another which, where correct treatment of language does not balance it into beautiful proportion, can become hostile to rhythm, in that the calm prevalence of time-measure does not always succeed in maintaining its right beside the vehemence of speech or the sharply accentuating understanding. The predominance of aesthetic feeling, which can however find obstacles in one-sidedness as well as in crudity, is decisive here; it preserves its freedom beside the emphasis of the combination of thoughts, and assigns to accent, even in the word, its place fitting for rhythmical euphony.

But since vowels determine the syllable, and can also form one on their own, the feeling for the syllable also affects the completeness of the alphabet, in which either all vowel sounds occur cleanly distinguished, each in its long or short form, or they do not. Written signs alone, however, cannot decide this. Thus, in the case of Sanskrit, it remains uncertain whether the living language also possessed a short e and o. Even individual dispositions and habits can exert only a lesser influence on it, since, for example, the meeting of several sounds must necessarily require more time in pronunciation. By contrast, disposition, habit and intention can favour or restrict the full effect of quantity in a language’s speech; from this arises a difference of the greatest importance for the euphony and rhythmic beauty of speech and of language generally, including their effect on character. The expression of thoughts is less fundamentally affected by this rhythmic peculiarity of language. Even excessive favour shown to quantity can never harm the expression of thoughts; unwarranted neglect can do so only insofar as a failure to distinguish long and short vowels carefully brings with it the same disadvantage as obscuring the pure sound of letters in general. On the other hand, suppressing the natural effect of quantity may well give the expression of thought an excessively one-sided prominence. For rhythm and accent stand in a relation that can become hostile to the former wherever proper handling of language fails to bring it into a beautiful balance, since quantity, in its quiet sway, does not always manage to assert its right alongside the vehemence of speech or the sharply accentuating understanding. The predominance of aesthetic feeling, which can meet with obstacles in one-sidedness just as much as in crudity, is decisive here: it preserves the freedom of rhythm alongside the emphasis of the connection of thoughts, and assigns accent, even within the word, its place in keeping with rhythmic euphony.

text_version.body: So wie das Zeitmass grösstentheils der eigenthümlichen Natur der Töne, so gehört der Accent ausschliesslich der Absicht des Redenden an. Er ist das Mittel, durch welches die Sprache die Rede, welche, ohne ihn, aus bloss an einander gereihten Grundtheilen bestehen würde, in verschiedene neben- und untergeordnete Ganze verknüpft und absondert. Denn indem der Accent eine Sylbe betont, macht er die folgenden tonlos, zieht sie daher in das Gebiet der betonten, und verbindet sie mithin mit derselben. Ebendies geschieht, wenn man Sylben, welche der Betonung vorausgehen, so an einander reihet, dass das Ohr durch die ihnen mangelnde Betonung auf eine zu erwartende aufmerksam wird. Dagegen schafft der Accent verschiedene Tongebiete und trennt die Sylben, indem er eine neue Betonung anheben lässt. Er folgt hierin unmittelbar der Richtung des Gedanken, und dient, den Fluss der Rede dem Fluss der Gedanken ähnlich zu machen, aber er wird bedingt durch die Gesetze der Aussprache, und fügt sich, jedoch mehr oder weniger, denen des Wohllauts. Man darf aber den Accent in diesem Sinne nicht mit andren Lautveränderungen der Vocale verwechseln, die wohl auch durch Accentzeichen angedeutet werden, und auch in Hebung oder Senkung der Stimme bestehen. Diese sind nur bestimmt durch Verschiedenheit der Intonation eine grössere Anzahl von Lauten möglich zu machen, als die intonationfreie Beschaffenheit derselben herzugeben vermag. Dies ist der Fall mit den Chinesischen Accentzeichen, da es im Chinesischen eigentlich so viele Abarten jedes Vocals giebt, als der Vocal Intonationen annehmen kann. Denn im Grunde fällt die Intonation der Sylbe doch immer nur auf den Vocal. Durch diese Intonationen vermehrt sich mithin der Umfang des Alphabets.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §66 — checked German

text_version.body: Just as temporal measure belongs for the most part to the peculiar nature of tones, so accent belongs exclusively to the speaker’s intention. It is the means through which language links and separates discourse, which without it would consist merely of fundamental parts strung together, into distinct coordinate and subordinate wholes. For by accentuating one syllable, accent makes the following syllables unaccented, thereby drawing them into the domain of the accented syllable and thus joining them to it. The same happens when syllables preceding the accentuation are strung together in such a way that their lack of accentuation alerts the ear to an accentuation to be expected. Conversely, accent creates different domains of tone and separates syllables by allowing a new accentuation to begin. In this it follows the direction of thought immediately, and serves to make the flow of discourse resemble the flow of thoughts; but it is conditioned by the laws of pronunciation and conforms, though to a greater or lesser degree, to those of euphony. Accent in this sense must not, however, be confused with other changes in the sound of vowels, which may likewise be indicated by accent marks and likewise consist in raising or lowering the voice. These are intended only to make possible, through differences of intonation, a greater number of sounds than their character without intonation can provide. This is the case with Chinese accent marks, since in Chinese there are, properly speaking, as many varieties of each vowel as the vowel can assume intonations. For fundamentally the intonation of the syllable always falls on the vowel alone. Through these intonations, therefore, the range of the alphabet increases.

text_version.body: Just as time-measure belongs for the most part to the peculiar nature of the tones, so accent belongs exclusively to the speaker's intention. It is the means by which language connects and separates speech, which without it would consist of fundamental parts merely strung together, into different co-ordinate and subordinate wholes. For by accentuating a syllable, accent makes the following syllables toneless, thus draws them into the domain of the accentuated one, and consequently connects them with it. The same happens when one strings together syllables preceding the accentuation in such a way that the ear, through the accentuation they lack, is made attentive to one to be expected. On the other hand, accent creates different tone-domains and separates the syllables by letting a new accentuation begin. In this it follows immediately the direction of thought and serves to make the flow of speech like the flow of thoughts, but it is conditioned by the laws of pronunciation and submits, though more or less, to those of euphony. But accent in this sense must not be confused with other sound-changes of the vowels, which may indeed also be indicated by accent signs and also consist in raising or lowering of the voice. These are intended only to make possible, through difference of intonation, a greater number of sounds than the character of those sounds, free of intonation, can yield. This is the case with the Chinese accent signs, since in Chinese there are properly as many varieties of each vowel as the vowel can assume intonations. For fundamentally the intonation of the syllable always falls only on the vowel after all. Through these intonations, consequently, the extent of the alphabet increases.

text_version.body: Just as quantity belongs for the most part to the particular nature of sounds, so accent belongs exclusively to the speaker’s intention. It is the means by which language joins and divides speech into different coordinate and subordinate wholes; without it, speech would consist merely of basic parts strung together. For by accenting one syllable, accent makes those that follow unaccented, thereby drawing them into the domain of the accented syllable and thus joining them to it. The same thing happens when syllables preceding the accent are strung together in such a way that their lack of accent alerts the ear to an accent still to come. Conversely, accent creates different domains of sound and separates the syllables by initiating a new accentuation. Here it follows the direction of thought immediately and serves to make the flow of speech resemble the flow of thoughts; but it is conditioned by the laws of pronunciation and submits, though to a greater or lesser degree, to those of euphony. Accent in this sense must not, however, be confused with other changes in vowel sounds that are likewise indicated by accent marks and likewise consist in raising or lowering the voice. These are intended only to make possible, through differences of intonation, a greater number of sounds than the nature of those sounds without intonation can yield. This is the case with Chinese accent marks, since in Chinese there are, properly speaking, as many varieties of each vowel as there are intonations the vowel can take. For at bottom, the intonation of a syllable always falls only on its vowel. These intonations thus increase the range of the alphabet.

text_version.body: Just as quantity belongs for the most part to the particular nature of sounds, so accent belongs exclusively to the speaker’s intention. For by accenting one syllable, accent makes those that follow unaccented, thereby drawing them into the domain of the accented syllable and thus joining them to it. The same thing happens when syllables preceding the accent are strung together in such a way that their lack of accent alerts the ear to an accent still to come. text_version.body: Die wichtigste Art des wahren Accents und diejenige, welche am meisten der Sprache angehört, ist der Wortaccent. Der Redeaccent wechselt natürlich nach der Beschaffenheit der Rede und kann nicht an den Theilen der unverbundenen Sprache haften. Aber seine Behandlung im Ganzen gehört allerdings zu der Natur der Sprache. Sie liegt zwar in der der Nation eigenthümlichen Vorstellungs- und Empfindungsweise, allein die Sprache kann von dieser auch niemals getrennt werden, und besteht, ausser den gleichsam todten Elementen, immer zugleich aus der in der Seele der Redenden liegenden Eigenthümlichkeit des lebendigen Vortrags, nur dass sich dieser an todten Sprachen gar nicht, oder wenigstens nur unvollkommen erkennen lässt. In der Sanskrita Sprache fehlen bis jetzt alle Nachrichten über die Accentuation, und wenn die der Griechischen sich auch in ihren Zeichen erhalten hat, so bleiben über die Art des lebendigen wirklichen Vortrags der Accente in Verbindung einerseits mit dem Redeaccent, andrerseits mit dem Zeitmass noch viele Zweifel übrig.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §67 — checked German

text_version.body: The most important kind of true accent, and the one that belongs most fully to language, is word accent. Discourse accent naturally varies with the character of the discourse and cannot adhere to the parts of language outside their connection in discourse. But its treatment as a whole certainly belongs to the nature of the language. This treatment admittedly lies in the nation’s distinctive way of representing things and feeling, but language can never be separated from this either, and, besides its as it were dead elements, always consists also in the distinctive character of living delivery that lies in the souls of its speakers; only, in dead languages this delivery cannot be discerned at all, or at least only imperfectly. For Sanskrit, all information about accentuation is so far lacking; and although Greek accentuation has been preserved in its signs, many doubts remain about the manner of the living, actual delivery of the accents in conjunction with discourse accent on the one hand and temporal measure on the other.

text_version.body: Das Wort entsteht erst durch den Accent, der ihm die Einheit des Begriffes einhaucht. Wenn sich in einem einfachen Worte zwei ganz gleiche Betonungen fänden, so stellte sich die Einheit des Begriffs nicht sinnlich auch vor dem Ohre dar, und die Angemessenheit der Begleitung des Gedanken durch den Laut wäre gestört. Das natürliche Sprachgefühl würde dadurch zu sehr verletzt, als dass man sich den Fall möglich denken könnte. Zwei in einem Worte aus zwei verschiedenen zusammenkommende Accente werden sich daher in der Aussprache einer dem andren unterordnen, oder die Begriffe der einzelnen Wörter müssten sich denn nicht in Einen verbinden; denn alsdann waltet nothwendig ein Element vor. Da der Accent durch die feste Stelle, die er im Worte einnimmt, dessen Individualität vollenden hilft, so können durch Verschiedenheit der Betonung aus der gleichen Sylbenfolge verschiedene Wörter entstehen, und es darf nicht in Verwunderung setzen, dass dies auch in Sprachen ganz ungebildeter Nationen angetroffen wird. Es ist eine sehr gewöhnliche Bemerkung, dass den Fremden bei den gemeinsten Volksklassen nichts so unverständlich macht, als unrichtige Betonung. Gerade der Ungebildete in Nationen und Ständen ist gewohnt, jedes Wort unzergliedert als ein Ganzes zu nehmen, dessen Physiognomie, wenn man so sagen darf, er an dem Accente erkennt.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §68 — checked German

text_version.body: The word comes into being only through accent, which breathes into it the unity of the concept. If a simple word contained two entirely equal accentuations, the unity of the concept would not also be presented to the ear through the senses, and the appropriateness of sound’s accompaniment of thought would be disturbed. This would violate the natural feeling for language too greatly for one to conceive the case as possible. Two accents coming together in one word from two different words will therefore be subordinated one to the other in pronunciation, unless the concepts of the individual words fail to combine into one; for when they do combine, one element necessarily predominates. Since accent, through the fixed place it occupies in the word, helps to complete the word’s individuality, different words can arise from the same sequence of syllables through differences of accentuation, and it should occasion no surprise that this is also found in the languages of entirely uncultivated nations. It is a very common observation that nothing makes a foreigner so unintelligible to the lowest classes of the people as incorrect accentuation. It is precisely the uncultivated person, among nations and social ranks alike, who is accustomed to taking each word, unanalysed, as a whole whose physiognomy, if one may put it so, is recognised by its accent.

text_version.body: Obgleich mehrere Worte eigentlich bloss durch den Redeaccent verbunden werden, so geschieht dies in einigen Fällen doch auch durch den wahren Sprachaccent, nur dass alsdann die verbundenen Theile nicht, wie in jenem Fall, ihre ihnen eigenthümlichen Accente unverändert erhalten. Man sieht leicht, dass ich hier an die enklitischen Wörter erinnern will, die es aber bei weitem nicht bloss im Griechischen, sondern wenn man genau darauf achtet, in allen Sprachen giebt und geben muss. Denn in allen ist der Fall vorhanden, dass für sich bestehende Wörter in eine solche Lage gegen andre treten, dass ihre selbständige Geltung ganz in der Anschliessung an diese aufgeht. Damit aber fällt von selbst auch ihre eigenthümliche Betonung dahin. In der so scharf accentuirten Englischen Sprache hört man dies, und zwar gerade auch im Volk, ungemein stark, und so dass die ganze Lautgeltung der enklitischen Wörter dadurch verändert wird. Wie dadurch auch der Accent des an sich reissenden Worts eine andre Stelle oder einen zweiten, jedoch wohl nicht gleich starken Accent neben sich erhalten kann, beruht auf Regeln und Gewohnheiten einzelner Sprachen, so wie auch, ob es für die Gattung von Wörtern, die angehängt werden können, doppelte Lautformen, eine orthotonische und enklitische, geben soll. Da in der Sanskrita Sprache zu dem Wort- und Redeaccent noch die genaue Bewahrung des Zeitmasses und die Wortverkettung durch Buchstabenveränderung hinzukam, so muss, bei dem ausserdem so grossen Umfange des Alphabets, ihr Lautsystem vorzüglich schwierig, aber auch ungemein reich und mannigfaltig gewesen seyn.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §69 — checked German

text_version.body: Although several words are properly joined only through discourse accent, in some cases they are also joined through true linguistic accent, except that the connected parts then do not retain their own accents unchanged, as they do in the former case. It is easy to see that I mean here to recall enclitic words, which, however, exist by no means only in Greek, but, if one attends closely, exist and must exist in all languages. For in all languages there are cases in which words that stand independently enter into such a relation to others that their independent force is wholly absorbed in their attachment to them. With this, their own distinctive accentuation also falls away of itself. In the so sharply accentuated English language, this can be heard with extraordinary force, precisely among the common people too, and in such a way that the entire sound value of the enclitic words is thereby altered. How this can also cause the accent of the word that draws the other to itself to occupy a different position, or to acquire beside it a second accent, though probably not an equally strong one, depends on the rules and habits of individual languages; so too does whether the kind of words that can be attached is to have two sound forms, an orthotonic and an enclitic one. Since Sanskrit added to word accent and discourse accent the exact preservation of temporal measure and the chaining of words through letter change, its sound system, with the already very great range of its alphabet, must have been particularly difficult, but also extraordinarily rich and manifold.

text_version.body: Although several words are properly connected only by speech-accent, in some cases this does also happen through true language-accent, except that then the connected parts do not, as in the former case, retain unchanged the accents peculiar to them. One sees easily that I wish here to recall enclitic words, which however exist very far from only in Greek; rather, if one attends closely to it, they exist and must exist in all languages. For in all of them the case occurs that words existing by themselves enter into such a position in relation to others that their independent validity is wholly absorbed in their attaching themselves to these. But with that their peculiar accentuation also falls away of itself. In English, accentuated so sharply, one hears this extremely strongly, and precisely also among the common people, and in such a way that the whole sound-validity of the enclitic words is thereby changed. How the accent of the word that pulls the other to itself can thereby also receive another place, or beside itself a second, though probably not equally strong, accent, rests on rules and habits of individual languages, as does also whether there are to be, for the class of words that can be attached, double sound-forms, an orthotonic and an enclitic one. Since in the Sanskrit language, in addition to word-accent and speech-accent, there were also exact preservation of time-measure and word-chaining through letter-change, its sound system, with the otherwise so great extent of the alphabet, must have been especially difficult but also extremely rich and manifold.

How this may also cause the accent of the word that pulls the other to itself to shift position, or to acquire a second accent beside it, though probably not one of equal strength, depends on the rules and habits of individual languages; so too does whether the kind of words that can be attached is to have two sound forms, one orthotonic and one enclitic. Since Sanskrit added to word accent and discourse accent the exact preservation of quantity and the chaining of words through letter change, its sound system, given the already very great range of its alphabet, must have been especially difficult, but also extraordinarily rich and varied.

text_version.body: Although several words are, properly speaking, joined together only by discourse accent, in some cases this also happens through true language accent; in that case, however, the joined parts do not retain their own accents unchanged, as they do in the former case. It is easy to see that I am referring here to enclitic words, which, however, are by no means confined to Greek: if one pays close attention, they exist, and must exist, in all languages. For in all languages there are cases in which words that stand on their own enter into such a relation to others that their independent standing is wholly absorbed in their attachment to those others. With this, their own accentuation also falls away of itself. In the sharply accented English language this can be heard with extraordinary force, indeed among the common people too, and in such a way that the entire sound value of the enclitic words is changed by it. How this may also cause the accent of the word that pulls the other to itself to shift position, or to acquire a second accent beside it, though probably not one of equal strength, depends on the rules and habits of individual languages; so too does whether the kind of words that can be attached is to have two sound forms, one orthotonic and one enclitic. text_version.body: Durch den Redeaccent kann der Sprechende entweder genau das Gewicht bezeichnen, welches jedes Wort und jeder Satz in der Bedeutung der Rede haben, oder die Erhebungen und Senkungen der Stimme nach einer davon unabhängigen in der Sprache zur Gewohnheit gewordenen Methode vertheilen, welcher die Rücksicht auf den Sinn zwar nicht ganz aufgeopfert, aber doch vollkommen untergeordnet wird. Dieser Unterschied zeigt sich am deutlichsten im Deutschen und Französischen Lesen und Declamiren, da die Franzosen den Deutschen, welcher ihre Sprache, wie die seinige, im Reden accentuirt, des Singens beschuldigen. Ausser diesen beiden sehr entgegengesetzten Arten giebt es indess viele minder bestimmt nuancirte, die sich alle durch das mehr, oder minder starke Herausheben der Verstandesgeltung der Wörter und Sylben unterscheiden, da wohl jedes Volk hierin einem eignen Gefühl folgt. Gerade aber weil es von dem wichtigsten Einfluss ist, auf welche Weise die Gedankenfolge in dem lebendigen Vortrage erscheint; so ist dieser Punkt von der grossesten Erheblichkeit für die intellectuelle Bildung, vorzüglich des am meisten auf die lebendige Mittheilung beschränkten Volks.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §70 — checked German

text_version.body: Through discourse accent, the speaker can either mark exactly the weight each word and each sentence has in the meaning of the discourse, or distribute the raisings and lowerings of the voice according to a method independent of that meaning that has become habitual in the language, to which regard for the sense is admittedly not entirely sacrificed, but is nevertheless completely subordinated. This difference appears most clearly in German and French reading and declamation, since the French accuse a German who accentuates their language in speaking as he does his own of singing. Besides these two strongly opposed kinds, however, there are many with less sharply defined nuances, all differing in how strongly they bring out the force of words and syllables for the understanding, since each people probably follows a feeling of its own in this. But precisely because the manner in which the sequence of thoughts appears in living delivery has the most important influence, this point is of the greatest significance for intellectual cultivation, especially that of the common people, who are most confined to living communication.

text_version.body: Through speech-accent the speaker can either designate exactly the weight which each word and each sentence is to have in the meaning of the speech, or distribute the risings and fallings of the voice according to a method, independent of that, that has become habitual in the language, to which regard for sense is indeed not wholly sacrificed but yet completely subordinated. This difference shows itself most clearly in German and French reading and declaiming, since the French accuse a German who accentuates their language in speaking as he does his own of singing. Besides these two very opposite kinds, however, there are many less definitely nuanced ones, all of which are distinguished by the more or less strong bringing out of the validity of words and syllables for the understanding, since probably every people follows its own feeling in this. But precisely because it is of the most important influence in what way the sequence of thoughts appears in living delivery, this point is of the greatest moment for intellectual cultivation, especially of the people most restricted to living communication.

text_version.body: Von den grossesten und sichtbarsten Folgen für die Ausbildung des Lautsystems ist die Einführung der Buchstabenschrift. Obgleich der articulirte Ton durch dieselbe niemals dem Gebiete des immer vergehenden Schalles entzogen wird, und nichts, als ein an diesen Schall erinnerndes Zeichen erhält, so wirken diese Zeichen und ihre Vergleichung doch dergestalt auf den Verstand und die Einbildungskraft, dass die Sprachtöne sich bestimmter an die ihnen angewiesenen Punkte heften, und viel klarer in ihrer Elementareigenschaft vor die Seele treten. An den Zeichen geht die Aussprache einer Generation auf die der andren über, und Abweichungen lassen sich an der Rechtschreibung erkennen, und die Sprachlaute können mit Allem, was zu ihnen gehört, Gegenstand der Betrachtung und der wissenschaftlichen Behandlung werden. Die Buchstabenschrift führt daher die beiden grossen Vorzüge mit sich, aus welchen sich hernach viele einzelne Folgen durch die ganze Sprache erstrecken : einmal dass alle Lautverhältnisse der Sprache sich reiner und bestimmter gegen einander stellen und ordnen, und vollständiger und systematischer ausgebildet werden, dann dass, indem der Verstand die Grundtheile der Sprache genauer trennt und bestimmter festhält, die Idee ihrer Gliederung lebendiger in ihm wird, und die Vorstellung ihres von den Grundtheilen an aufsteigenden Baues an Anschaulichkeit und Vollständigkeit gewinnt. Dagegen kann auch durch die wissenschaftliche Bearbeitung der Lautbezeichnungen zu gekünstelte und systematische Behandlung derselben vorzüglich da entstehen, wo Sprachen aus dem lebendigen Volksverkehr in bloss gelehrten Gebrauch überzugehen anfangen.

text_version.body: The introduction of alphabetic writing has consequences of the greatest and most visible kind for the development of the sound system. Although it never removes articulated tone from the realm of sound that is forever passing away, and gives it nothing but a sign recalling that sound, these signs and their comparison nevertheless act upon the understanding and the imagination in such a way that speech tones attach themselves more definitely to their assigned points and appear before the soul much more clearly in their character as elements. Through the signs, the pronunciation of one generation passes to that of another; deviations can be recognised in spelling, and speech sounds, with everything belonging to them, can become objects of reflection and scholarly treatment. Alphabetic writing therefore brings with it two great advantages, from which many particular consequences subsequently extend throughout the language: first, all the sound relations of the language are set against one another and ordered more purely and definitely, and are developed more completely and systematically; second, as the understanding separates the fundamental parts of language more exactly and holds them more definitely, the idea of its articulation becomes more vivid within it, and the representation of its structure, rising from the fundamental parts upwards, gains in intuitive clarity and completeness. On the other hand, scholarly work on the signs for sounds can also give rise to an excessively artificial and systematic treatment of them, especially where languages begin to pass from living intercourse among the people into exclusively learned use.

text_version.body: Of the greatest and most visible consequences for the development of the sound system is the introduction of alphabetic writing. Although articulated tone is never thereby withdrawn from the domain of ever-passing sound, and receives nothing but a sign recalling this sound, these signs and their comparison nevertheless act on the understanding and the imagination in such a way that the tones of language attach themselves more definitely to the points assigned to them, and step before the soul much more clearly in their elementary character. By means of the signs, the pronunciation of one generation passes over to that of another, deviations can be recognized in the spelling, and speech sounds, with all that belongs to them, can become an object of contemplation and of scientific treatment. Alphabetic writing therefore brings with it the two great advantages from which afterwards many individual consequences extend through the whole language: first, that all sound relations of language place and arrange themselves more purely and definitely in relation to one another and are developed more completely and systematically; then, that, as the understanding separates the fundamental parts of language more exactly and holds them more definitely fast, the idea of their articulation becomes more living in it, and the representation of their structure, ascending from the fundamental parts, gains in intuitive vividness and completeness. On the other hand, through scientific working on the sound designations, an excessively artificial and systematic treatment of them can also arise, especially where languages begin to pass from living intercourse among the people into merely learned use.

text_version.body: In den Chinesischen Grammatiken werden die Intonationen zwar Modificationen der Wörter, oder was dort auf Eins hinausläuft, der Sylben genannt, was auch in ihnen viel zweckmässiger ist. Allein eigentlich ruhen sie doch nur auf der Vocalendung, und daher ist es, nach Art andrer Sprachen zu reden, natürlicher zu sagen, dass jede einfache und zusammengesetzte Vocalendung diese und diese Intonation haben kann, und nun die Wörter, nach Verschiedenheit ihrer Bedeutung, die so oder so intonirte Vocalendung annehmen. Auf diese Weise stellt sich die Sache den kurzen und langen Vocalen anderer Sprachen gleich.

text_version.body: Humboldt’s note: In Chinese grammars, intonations are admittedly called modifications of words, or, what there amounts to the same thing, of syllables, which is also much more appropriate in those grammars. Yet strictly speaking they rest only on the vowel ending, and it is therefore more natural, speaking in the manner of other languages, to say that each simple and compound vowel ending can have such and such an intonation, and that words then adopt a vowel ending intoned in one way or another according to differences in their meaning. Viewed in this way, the matter is placed on the same footing as the short and long vowels of other languages.

Yet, properly speaking, they rest only on the vowel ending; hence, speaking in the manner of other languages, it is more natural to say that each simple and compound vowel ending can have such and such an intonation, and that the words then take the vowel ending intoned in this or that way according to differences in their meaning. In this way the matter is put on the same footing as the short and long vowels of other languages.
